Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments

Siqi He    Yehua Wei    Jiaming Xu
Abstract

We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by ss, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1−O⁡(1/s)1-O(1/s) at every scale s≥1s\geq 1 and every horizon T≥1T\geq 1, so the ratio tends to 11 as ss goes to infinity.

1 Introduction

In dynamic matching markets, waiting can create opportunities for more valuable matches, but it can also lead to costly delays and abandonment. This tradeoff arises in a variety of operational settings, including kidney exchange, ride-sharing platforms, and online dating platforms (Özkan and Ward, 2020; Ashlagi et al., 2023; Rios et al., 2023; Kohlenberg and Gurvich, 2025). To understand how to manage this tradeoff, researchers have studied dynamic matching models in which agents of different types arrive over time and a matching network specifies which types of agents can be paired. In such models, a decision maker observes the agents currently in the system and decides which matches to make and which agents to leave waiting. Each match generates a reward, and matched agents leave the market. Unmatched agents incur holding costs per unit of time and abandon the market with a penalty when their waiting times exceed their patience times. The objective of the decision maker is to maximize expected total matching rewards net of holding costs and abandonment penalties.

One stream of research on dynamic matching with abandonment focuses on policies with constant-factor guarantees for long-run average performance (Collina et al., 2020; Aouad and Saritaç, 2022; AmaniHamedani et al., 2024). These guarantees bound the loss relative to optimal performance, but leave a fixed approximation gap. Recently, AmaniHamedani et al. (2025) made significant progress by developing policies that can make this gap arbitrarily small for bipartite matching models with a fixed number of waiting agent types. However, their model assumes waiting on only one side of the market, while agents on the other side must be matched immediately upon arrival or leave unmatched. In addition, the policies are also complex, making them difficult to implement in practice. This motivates the search for simple policies with near-optimal performance in markets where agents of all types can wait and abandon.

The high-volume regime offers a promising setting for developing such policies. Also known as the large-market regime, it has proved useful for analyzing simple policies (Akbarpour et al., 2020; Blanchet et al., 2022) and for guiding policy design (Özkan and Ward, 2020; Ata and Xu, 2025) in various dynamic matching markets. In the high-volume regime, the arrival rates of all agent types grow proportionally with a market-size parameter, denoted by ss. Aveklouris et al. (2025) study bipartite matching markets in which agents on both sides can wait and abandon. They show that simple matching policies can achieve an approximation ratio converging to 1 as the market grows, under a long-run average objective.11 1 Their asymptotic guarantee first takes the market-size parameter s→∞s\to\infty and then the time horizon T→∞T\to\infty. Their policies make matches at scheduled review times with review intervals proportional to s−2/3s^{-2/3}, allowing the expected number of arrivals between reviews to grow as s1/3s^{1/3} as the market grows. Their analysis also accommodates non-exponential patience-time distributions.

In contrast to the long-run asymptotic optimality guarantees for bipartite matching in Aveklouris et al. (2025), we establish explicit performance bounds at a given market size ss and over a finite operating horizon TT. We consider general two-way matching networks, including those that are non-bipartite, with exponentially distributed patience times. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the fluid LP’s unique optimal dual solution to remain optimal under small perturbations of arrival rates, we show that a simple longest-queue policy achieves an approximation ratio of at least 1−C/s1-C/s relative to the optimal policy, for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T≥1T\geq 1, where CC is independent of ss and TT. Without GPG, the same policy remains asymptotically optimal, with a weaker bound of O⁡(1/s)O(1/\sqrt{s}) on the approximation gap. In addition to the theoretical guarantees, the key difference between our longest-queue policy and the discrete-review policies of Aveklouris et al. (2025) is that the longest-queue policy makes matching decisions immediately upon each arrival, avoiding the additional waiting imposed by scheduled reviews and requiring no choice of a review interval. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the practical value of this approach, as the longest-queue policy achieves higher approximation ratios than both discrete-review benchmarks across the tested instances, market sizes, and review intervals.

The longest-queue policy we propose is guided by a fluid linear program that provides an upper bound on achievable performance. The fluid formulation is adapted from the fluid models for overloaded queueing systems with abandonment (Whitt, 2006; Atar et al., 2010), as it balances arrival rates against matching and abandonment rates, with exponential patience making abandonment flows linear in queue lengths. Before matching begins, we use its optimal dual solution to identify a set of good match types to use and a set of critical agent types to prioritize. These sets remain fixed throughout the operating horizon, so the policy does not need to solve the linear program after the horizon starts. Upon each arrival, it considers available partners that form a good match. If any critical partners are available, it selects one from the type with the longest queue. Otherwise, it matches with an available noncritical partner that forms a good match, if one exists. If no good match is available, the arriving agent waits. We note that restricting immediate matching to a selected set of compatible pairs is also central to the restricted-greedy policies of Kohlenberg (2024), studied in bipartite markets with demand-dependent rewards.

Our analysis builds upon two simple yet key observations. First, under exponential patience times, the expected cumulative abandonment is the time integral of expected queue length. Controlling queues therefore controls both holding costs and abandonment penalties. Second, after rewriting the objective in terms of adjusted match rewards, complementary slackness and the policy’s restriction to good matches yield an exact regret representation involving only critical types. In particular, noncritical queues may be large, and their aggregate abandonment rates may scale with ss, but their zero dual prices ensure that they do not contribute to the regret. The analysis therefore reduces to bounding the expected critical queue length uniformly in time and the market-size parameter ss. Such a bound keeps the expected loss per unit time bounded, while the fluid benchmark grows proportionally with ss, yielding the O⁡(1/s)O(1/s) relative performance gap.

To establish the desired uniform bound on critical queue lengths, we adapt a standard Lyapunov-drift argument used in recent work establishing constant regret in discrete-time dynamic matching models without abandonment. Although abandonment contributes a nonpositive term to the drift of the quadratic Lyapunov function, this contribution does not scale with ss at a fixed queue size and hence cannot by itself yield a queue bound uniform in ss. Instead, we apply the analysis of Kerimov et al. (2025) to show that, under the GPG condition, the longest-queue policy generates negative drift of order ss whenever the critical-queue norm exceeds a threshold independent of ss. Thus, the longest-queue policy provides the drift needed to control critical queues as the market grows, and abandonment can only strengthen this drift.

The remaining challenge is to convert this negative-drift condition into a bound that is uniform over all times. The standard stochastic comparison arguments used in the matching literature, e.g., Gupta (2024); Kerimov et al. (2025), do not directly extend because abandonment intensities depend on the current queues, so systems initialized in different states generally have different departure dynamics. Building on the drift method of Hajek (1982), we instead analyze an exponential Lyapunov function for the continuous-time jump process. Although the aggregate abandonment rate may be unbounded, these jumps only decrease the critical queues. For these downward jumps, we absorb the quadratic remainder of the exponential increment into its negative first-order contribution. Upward jumps are controlled by the state-independent aggregate arrival rate. This yields an affine drift inequality for the exponential Lyapunov function, and Dynkin’s formula together with Grönwall’s inequality gives the desired critical-queue bound uniformly in both time and ss.

2 Model Setup

We consider a finite set of agent types 𝒩=[n]={1,…,n}\mathcal{N}=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\} and a finite set of match types ℳ=[d]={1,…,d}\mathcal{M}=[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}. We assume that each match type is two-way, that is, m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} is determined by two distinct types i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] such that 𝒩⁡(m)≜{i,j}\mathcal{N}(m)\triangleq\{i,j\}. Throughout this paper, we use mm and (i,j)(i,j) interchangeably. The match types can be alternatively represented as a network adjacency matrix M∈{0,1}n×dM\in\{0,1\}^{n\times d}, where Mi​m=𝟏{i∈𝒩(m)}M_{im}=\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{N}(m)\}.

The system maintains a separate, initially empty queue for each agent type i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N}. Type-ii agents arrive and join the corresponding queue according to a Poisson process with rate λi>0\lambda_{i}>0, where λ=(λ1,…,λn)⊤\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n})^{\top}. Upon arrival, each type-ii agent draws a patience time from the exponential distribution with rate θi>0\theta_{i}>0, independently of all other agents and of the arrival processes, where θ=(θ1,…,θn)⊤\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})^{\top}. Executing a match of type mm pairs one agent of each type in 𝒩⁡(m)\mathcal{N}(m) and removes both agents from the queues. The value of performing a type-mm match is rm≥0r_{m}\geq 0. If an agent waits longer than its patience time, it abandons the system. A type-ii agent incurs holding cost cic_{i} per unit of time while waiting and an abandonment penalty γi\gamma_{i} if it leaves without being matched.

We consider the class Π\Pi of admissible policies, where each π∈Π\pi\in\Pi is a sequence of (potentially randomized) actions whose action at each time tt is measurable with respect to the σ\sigma-field generated by the history of arrivals, abandonments, and matching decisions up to time tt. However, agents’ patience times are not observed before abandonments.

For each i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N} and t≥0t\geq 0, let Ai​(t)A_{i}(t) denote the cumulative number of type-ii arrivals by time tt. A match type m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} is available if the queues of both agent types in 𝒩⁡(m)\mathcal{N}(m) are nonempty. At each agent arrival time tt, policy π\pi uses the observed history to select a (possibly empty) collection of available matches. For each m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, let Xmπ​(t)X_{m}^{\pi}(t) denote the number of times match type mm has been performed by time tt under policy π\pi. Let Biπ​(t)B_{i}^{\pi}(t) denote the cumulative number of type-ii abandonments by time tt under policy π\pi.

Let qiπ​(t)q_{i}^{\pi}(t) denote the number of waiting type-ii agents at time tt under policy π\pi. All counting processes start at zero, and qiπ​(0)=0q_{i}^{\pi}(0)=0 for every i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N}. The queue length of each type satisfies

qiπ​(t)=Ai​(t)−∑m=1dMi​m​Xmπ​(t)−Biπ​(t),i∈𝒩,t≥0.q_{i}^{\pi}(t)=A_{i}(t)-\sum_{m=1}^{d}M_{im}X_{m}^{\pi}(t)-B_{i}^{\pi}(t),\qquad i\in\mathcal{N},\quad t\geq 0. (1)

For a queue vector q∈ℤ+nq\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n}, define the terminal inventory cost

Cterm​(q)≔∑i=1n(ciθi+γi)​qi.C^{\mathrm{term}}(q)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{c_{i}}{\theta_{i}}+\gamma_{i}\right)q_{i}.

This cost evaluates the system under the convention that matching stops at the terminal time and every remaining agent subsequently waits until abandonment. By the memoryless property of the exponential patience-time distribution, a remaining type-ii agent has expected residual patience time 1/θi1/\theta_{i}, so its expected post-horizon holding and abandonment cost is ci/θi+γic_{i}/\theta_{i}+\gamma_{i}.

For a horizon T>0T>0, the realized net value of a policy π\pi is

Fπ​(T)≔∑m=1drm​Xmπ​(T)−∑i=1nci​∫0Tqiπ​(t)​𝑑t−∑i=1nγi​Biπ​(T)−Cterm​(qπ​(T)).F^{\pi}(T)\coloneqq\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\int_{0}^{T}q_{i}^{\pi}(t)\,dt-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}B_{i}^{\pi}(T)-C^{\mathrm{term}}\!\left(q^{\pi}(T)\right). (2)

The decision maker seeks a policy that maximizes 𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)].

3 Fluid Benchmark and Regret

3.1 Fluid Relaxation

In this section we introduce a deterministic fluid relaxation of the stochastic matching model and the corresponding linear optimization problem, whose optimal value upper bounds 𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]/T\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]/T, the expected net value per unit time achieved by any admissible policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi.

In the fluid model, discrete arrivals and departures are replaced by continuous flows. Let x⁡(t)∈ℝ+dx(t)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d} denote the vector of matching rates, and q⁡(t)∈ℝ+nq(t)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} denote the vector of fluid queue lengths, started at q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0. Recalling that MM is the incidence matrix between agent types and match types, (M​x​(t))i(Mx(t))_{i} is the rate at which type-ii fluid is consumed by matching.

Type-ii fluid enters at the constant rate λi\lambda_{i} and leaves through two channels: it is matched at rate (M​x​(t))i(Mx(t))_{i}, and it abandons at intensity θi​qi​(t)\theta_{i}q_{i}(t). The fluid queue therefore evolves according to

q˙​(t)=λ−M​x​(t)−Θ​q​(t),Θ=diag⁡(θ1,…,θn),\dot{q}(t)=\lambda-Mx(t)-\Theta q(t),\qquad\Theta=\operatorname{diag}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}), (3)

and a matching-rate trajectory is admissible only if it keeps q⁡(t)≥0q(t)\geq 0 throughout.

Setting q˙​(t)=0\dot{q}(t)=0 in (3), a stationary point (x,q)(x,q) satisfies the flow-balance condition

M​x+Θ​q=λ.Mx+\Theta q=\lambda. (4)

This condition says that every agent who arrives eventually leaves, either through a match or through abandonment.

We now define the optimization problem over the pairs (x,q)(x,q) satisfying (4). Matching generates reward at rate r⊤​xr^{\top}x, and holding the queue costs c⊤​qc^{\top}q per unit time. In addition, type-ii fluid abandons at rate θi​qi\theta_{i}q_{i}, and each abandoning unit incurs the penalty γi\gamma_{i}, so abandonment penalties are incurred at rate ∑i=1nγi​θi​qi\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}\theta_{i}q_{i}. The latter two costs are both linear in qq, so we combine them into the abandonment-adjusted holding-cost vector

c¯i=ci+θi​γi,i∈[n],\overline{c}_{i}=c_{i}+\theta_{i}\gamma_{i},\qquad i\in[n], (5)

which leaves r⊤​x−c¯⊤​qr^{\top}x-\overline{c}^{\top}q as the objective, the net value generated per unit time. Maximizing it subject to (4) yields the static fluid benchmark

F∗​(λ)=[maxx,q∑m=1drm​xm−∑i=1nc¯i​qis.t.θiqi+(Mx)i=λi,i∈[n],x∈ℝ≥0d,q∈ℝ≥0n].\displaystyle F^{*}(\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}\max_{x,q}\quad&\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}x_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\overline{c}_{i}q_{i}\\ \text{s.t.}\quad&\theta_{i}q_{i}+(Mx)_{i}=\lambda_{i},\qquad i\in[n],\\ &x\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{d},\quad q\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\end{bmatrix}. (6)

The next lemma shows that the optimal value of (6) is an upper bound on the net value per unit time achieved by any admissible policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi.

Lemma 1 (Fluid Upper Bound).

For any admissible policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi,

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]T≤F∗​(λ).\frac{\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\leq F^{*}(\lambda).

The proof idea is as follows. Given π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, we use its expected matching rates and queue lengths per unit time to construct a feasible solution (x¯,q¯)(\overline{x},\overline{q}) to (6), whose objective value equals 𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]/T\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]/T. The bound then follows from the optimality of F∗​(λ)F^{*}(\lambda). The formal proof is deferred to Appendix A.

3.2 High-Volume Setting

In this paper, we study the performance of matching policies under a high-volume scaling in which the arrival rates of all agent types increase proportionally, while all other model primitives remain fixed. The scaling is expressed relative to a base arrival-rate vector λb∈ℝ+n\lambda^{b}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} satisfying ∑i=1nλib=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{b}=1. We next define the regime formally.

Definition 1 (High-volume regime).

We consider a family of systems indexed by s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}, where ss tends to infinity, and let the arrival rates in the ssth system be

λis=s​λibfor all ​i∈𝒩,or equivalentlyλs=s​λb.\lambda_{i}^{s}=s\lambda_{i}^{b}\quad\text{for all }i\in\mathcal{N},\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b}. (7)

Otherwise, each system ss has the same basic structure as the system described in Section 2.

In the high-volume regime, the fluid model in (3) serves as an accurate approximation to the discrete-event stochastic model of Section 2, whose dynamics are given by the flow balance equation (1). In addition to dynamic matching, similar fluid approximations have also been studied for multiserver queues with abandonment; see Whitt (2006).

3.3 Performance Measure

We evaluate matching policies by comparing their expected performance with the fluid upper bound. For each scale s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}, let Fsπ​(T)F_{s}^{\pi}(T) denote the net value generated by policy π\pi over the horizon [0,T][0,T] in the system with arrival-rate vector λs=s​λb\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b}, and define

Fs∗≔F∗​(λs).F_{s}^{*}\coloneqq F^{*}(\lambda^{s}).

Lemma 1 shows that the fluid value bounds from above the expected net value per unit time of every admissible policy:

𝔼​[Fsπ​(T)]T≤Fs∗,s∈ℕ,T>0,π∈Π.\frac{\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\leq F_{s}^{*},\qquad s\in\mathbb{N},\quad T>0,\quad\pi\in\Pi.

We therefore define regret as the gap between these two quantities.

Definition 2 (Time-average regret).

For a policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, its time-average regret at scale ss over horizon TT is

ℛT,sπ≔Fs∗−𝔼​[Fsπ​(T)]T≥0.\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}\coloneqq F_{s}^{*}-\frac{\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\geq 0.

We next introduce the performance measure used in this paper, the approximation ratio, which compares a policy with the fluid benchmark.

Definition 3 (Approximation ratio).

For a policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, its approximation ratio at scale ss over horizon TT is

ρT,sπ≔𝔼​[Fsπ​(T)]T​Fs∗≤1,\rho_{T,s}^{\pi}\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)]}{TF_{s}^{*}}\leq 1,

where the fluid value Fs∗F_{s}^{*} is assumed positive, and the inequality follows from Lemma 1.

By Definition 2,

ρT,sπ=1−ℛT,sπFs∗,\rho_{T,s}^{\pi}=1-\frac{\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}}{F_{s}^{*}},

so a bound on the time-average regret ℛT,sπ\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi} directly lower-bounds the approximation ratio.

4 Main Results

In this section, we develop the longest-queue policy and state its performance guarantee. We first rewrite the fluid program (6) in a reduced form and derive its dual, which provides a convenient basis for the policy design. The general position gap (GPG) condition, introduced next, plays a central role in our main result. Finally, we define the longest-queue policy and state its performance guarantee.

Throughout the paper, we use λ\lambda for a general arrival-rate vector. When a result depends explicitly on the high-volume scale ss, we write λs=s​λb\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b} and display that dependence explicitly.

4.1 Reduced Formulation and Dual

The fluid program (6) can be written solely in terms of the matching-rate vector xx, because the balance constraint (4) uniquely determines the queue-length vector as q=Θ−1​(λ−M​x)q=\Theta^{-1}(\lambda-Mx), and the nonnegativity requirement q≥0q\geq 0 is therefore equivalent to M​x≤λMx\leq\lambda. Substituting this expression for qq into the objective of (6) yields

r⊤​x−c¯⊤​q\displaystyle r^{\top}x-\overline{c}^{\top}q =r⊤​x−c¯⊤​Θ−1​(λ−M​x)\displaystyle=r^{\top}x-\overline{c}^{\top}\Theta^{-1}(\lambda-Mx)
=−λ⊤​Θ−1​c¯+(r+M⊤​Θ−1​c¯)⊤​x.\displaystyle=-\lambda^{\top}\Theta^{-1}\overline{c}+\bigl(r+M^{\top}\Theta^{-1}\overline{c}\bigr)^{\top}x.

For ease of notation, we define the adjusted match-reward vector by

r~=r+M⊤​Θ−1​c¯,r~m=rm+∑i=1nc¯iθi​Mi​m.\widetilde{r}=r+M^{\top}\Theta^{-1}\overline{c},\qquad\widetilde{r}_{m}=r_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}}{\theta_{i}}M_{im}. (8)

Using this notation, we obtain an alternative formulation of the linear program (6):

F∗​(λ)=[maxx∑m=1dr~m​xm−∑i=1nc¯i​λiθis.t.(Mx)i≤λi,i∈[n],x∈ℝ≥0d].\displaystyle F^{*}(\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}\max_{x}\quad&\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{d}\widetilde{r}_{m}x_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\overline{c}_{i}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\\ \text{s.t.}\quad&(Mx)_{i}\leq\lambda_{i},\qquad i\in[n],\\ &x\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{d}\end{bmatrix}. (9)

Then we derive the following dual formulation of (9):

F∗​(λ)=[minUU⊤​λ−∑i=1nc¯i​λiθis.t.∑i=1nUiMi​m≥r~m,m∈[d],U∈ℝ≥0n].\displaystyle F^{*}(\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}\min_{U}\quad&\displaystyle U^{\top}\lambda-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\overline{c}_{i}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\\ \text{s.t.}\quad&\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}M_{im}\geq\widetilde{r}_{m},\qquad m\in[d],\\ &U\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}\end{bmatrix}. (10)

After eliminating qq, the matching-rate vector xx is the only primal decision variable, and UU is the vector of dual multipliers associated with the constraint M​x≤λMx\leq\lambda. Let x∗x^{*} be an optimal solution of (9) and set q∗=Θ−1​(λ−M​x∗)q^{*}=\Theta^{-1}(\lambda-Mx^{*}); then (x∗,q∗)(x^{*},q^{*}) is optimal for (6). Throughout, we write U∗U^{*} for an optimal solution of the dual (10). Since x∗x^{*} is optimal for the reduced primal (9), the optimal objective value can be written as

F∗​(λ)=⟨r~,x∗⟩−∑i=1nc¯i​λiθi,F^{*}(\lambda)=\langle\widetilde{r},x^{*}\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}\lambda_{i}}{\theta_{i}}, (11)

which is also attained by (x∗,q∗)(x^{*},q^{*}) in the original formulation (6).

4.2 General Position Gap

Next, we introduce the notion of the general position gap (GPG), which measures how far the base arrival-rate vector λb\lambda^{b} can be perturbed while the unique optimal solution of the dual (10) remains optimal. We adopt the dual-based definition of Wei et al. (2026), which differs slightly from the general position gap condition of Kerimov et al. (2025): the latter requires the primal LP (9) to have a unique nondegenerate optimal solution, a stronger assumption. Consequently, the condition of Kerimov et al. (2025) implies a positive GPG defined below, whereas the converse need not hold.

Definition 4 (General Position Gap).

Let ℬε​(λb){\mathcal{B}}_{\varepsilon}(\lambda^{b}) denote the ℓ2\ell_{2}-ball of radius ε\varepsilon centered at λb\lambda^{b}, i.e., ℬε​(λb)={λ^:‖λ^−λb‖2≤ε}{\mathcal{B}}_{\varepsilon}(\lambda^{b})=\{\widehat{\lambda}:\|\widehat{\lambda}-\lambda^{b}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon\}. We say that λb\lambda^{b} has a GPG of at least ε>0\varepsilon>0 if (10) has a unique optimal solution U∗U^{*} and U∗U^{*} remains optimal when λb\lambda^{b} is replaced by any λ^∈ℬε​(λb)\widehat{\lambda}\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\varepsilon}(\lambda^{b}).

A positive GPG ensures that the optimizer U∗U^{*} of (10) is unique and remains optimal throughout a neighborhood of λb\lambda^{b}, so the match types it selects stay correct even when the realized arrival rates fluctuate around λb\lambda^{b}. We use this robustness to analyze the longest-queue policy proposed in Section 4.3.

4.3 The Longest-Queue Policy

We now describe our longest-queue policy, summarized in Algorithm 1. Before the system starts, we use the optimal dual solution U∗U^{*} of (10) to identify the sets of good matches and critical agent types, defined below. These sets remain fixed throughout the horizon. We say an agent type is critical if its dual variable is positive, and a match type is good if its dual constraint is binding. We define the sets of critical agent types and good match types as

ℐ+≔{i∈𝒩:Ui∗>0},ℳg≔{m∈ℳ:∑i=1nUi∗​Mi​m=r~m}.\mathcal{I}^{+}\coloneqq\{i\in\mathcal{N}:U_{i}^{*}>0\},\qquad\mathcal{M}^{g}\coloneqq\{m\in\mathcal{M}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}^{*}M_{im}=\widetilde{r}_{m}\}. (12)

For a type-ii arrival at time tt, define the sets of available critical and noncritical good neighbors of ii as

𝒩i+​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t) ≔{j∈ℐ+:qj(t)>0,(i,j)∈ℳg},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}:q_{j}(t)>0,\ (i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}\}, (13)
𝒩i0​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}^{0}(t) ≔{j∈𝒩∖ℐ+:qj(t)>0,(i,j)∈ℳg}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\{j\in\mathcal{N}\setminus\mathcal{I}^{+}:q_{j}(t)>0,\ (i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}\}. (14)

The system starts empty, q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0. At each arrival time tt, let x⁡(t)x(t) denote the matching decision. For a type-ii arrival, the policy selects j∗∈𝒩i+​(t)j^{*}\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t) with the longest queue, or j∗∈𝒩i0​(t)j^{*}\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{0}(t) if the former is empty, and sets x⁡(t)=e(i,j∗)x(t)=e_{(i,j^{*})}. If both sets are empty, it sets x⁡(t)=0x(t)=0, and the arrival joins queue ii.22 2 This ensures that our policy uses good matches whenever the agents are available, and thus no two waiting agents can ever form a good match. See Lemma 10 for the proof. Ties among longest queues and choices among noncritical types follow a deterministic rule fixed in advance, such as choosing the smallest index.

The intuition behind our policy is as follows. The optimal dual Uj∗U_{j}^{*} measures the marginal (shadow) value of type-jj supply for the optimal adjusted matching reward. For any match m=(i,j)m=(i,j), the dual feasibility gives r~m−Ui∗−Uj∗≤0\widetilde{r}_{m}-U_{i}^{*}-U_{j}^{*}\leq 0. If the inequality is strict, the match earns less reward than the shadow value it consumes, so the policy restricts attention to good matches, for which equality holds. Critical supply has positive shadow value, whereas noncritical supply has zero shadow value. The policy therefore prioritizes critical agents to limit the loss of valuable supply through abandonment. Among available critical partners, it serves the longest queue to help keep critical queues small.

Next, we formally quantify how the policy’s control of critical queues translates into performance relative to the fluid benchmark. Theorem 1 shows that, under the GPG condition, the longest-queue policy’s time-average regret is bounded by a constant independent of the market size ss and operating horizon TT, uniformly over s≥1s\geq 1 and T≥1T\geq 1. The bound also makes explicit its dependence on the number of agent types nn and the GPG parameter ε\varepsilon.

Theorem 1 (Average Regret Bound).

Suppose that the base arrival-rate vector λb\lambda^{b} satisfies the GPG condition in Definition 4 with the parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0. Let π=πLQ\pi=\pi^{\mathrm{LQ}} be the policy in Algorithm 1. Then, for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T≥1T\geq 1,

0≤ℛT,sπ≤C​nε​log⁡nε,0\;\leq\;\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}\;\leq\;C\,\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\,\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon},

where CC depends only on the abandonment rates θ\theta and the largest adjusted match reward r~max\widetilde{r}_{\max} (maxm∈ℳ⁡r~m)\bigl(\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\widetilde{r}_{m}\bigr). Explicitly, for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T>0T>0,

ℛT,sπ=Fs∗−𝔼​[Fsπ​(T)]T≤(1T+θmax)​n​r~max​ℬq​(s),\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}=F_{s}^{*}-\frac{\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\leq\left(\frac{1}{T}+\theta_{\max}\right)\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}\,\mathcal{B}_{q}(s),

where θmax=maxi⁡θi\theta_{\max}=\max_{i}\theta_{i} and

ℬq​(s)=\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{q}(s)= nε+(1+4​n​(e−32)ε)×ln⁡(2+4​nε+4​ns​ε2​∑i∈ℐ+θi2).\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\left(1+\frac{4\sqrt{n}\left(\mathrm{e}-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{\varepsilon}\right)\times\ln\left(2+\frac{4\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{4n}{s\varepsilon^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{I}}^{+}}\theta^{2}_{i}}\right).

In particular, ℬq​(s)\mathcal{B}_{q}(s) is non-increasing in ss, and

sups≥1ℬq​(s)=ℬq​(1)=O⁡(nε​log⁡nε).\sup_{s\geq 1}\mathcal{B}_{q}(s)=\mathcal{B}_{q}(1)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}\right).

The proof of Theorem 1 is presented in Section 5. Note that Theorem 1 immediately leads to the following lower bound on the approximation ratio.

Corollary 1 (Approximation Ratio).

Suppose the assumptions of Theorem 1 hold. Then

ρT,sπLQ≥1−Cs,\rho_{T,s}^{\pi^{\mathrm{LQ}}}\geq 1-\frac{C}{s},

where CC is a constant independent of TT and ss. It follows that the approximation ratio approaches 11 at rate 1/s1/s as s→∞s\to\infty.

Without the GPG condition, our longest-queue policy still achieves an approximation ratio that approaches 11, with a convergence guarantee of order 1/s1/\sqrt{s} rather than 1/s1/s. We present the formal result in Proposition 1.

Proposition 1 (Regret and Approximation Ratio without GPG).

For any optimal solution U∗U^{*} of (10) at the base arrival-rate vector λb\lambda^{b}, let π=πLQ\pi=\pi^{\mathrm{LQ}} be the policy in Algorithm 1. Then, for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T>0T>0,

0≤ℛT,sπ≤(1T+‖θ‖∞)​n​r~max​sθmin,0\leq\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}\leq\left(\frac{1}{T}+\|\theta\|_{\infty}\right)\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{s}{\theta_{\min}}}, (17)

where θmin=mini∈𝒩⁡θi\theta_{\min}=\min_{i\in\mathcal{N}}\theta_{i} and r~max=maxm∈ℳ⁡r~m\widetilde{r}_{\max}=\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\widetilde{r}_{m}. Moreover, for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T≥1T\geq 1,

ρT,sπ≥1−Cs,\rho_{T,s}^{\pi}\geq 1-\frac{C}{\sqrt{s}}, (18)

where CC is a constant independent of TT and ss.

The proof is given in Appendix C. Without GPG, matching contributes only a nonpositive drift term, while abandonment supplies the downward drift that yields the O⁡(s)O(\sqrt{s}) bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}]. This explains why the regret bound in Proposition 1 depends on 1/θmin1/\sqrt{\theta_{\min}} and does not extend directly to the non-abandonment setting.

Under GPG, the longest-queue rule itself generates a stronger matching-induced drift, improving the queue bound to O⁡(1)O(1) and the approximation gap from O⁡(1/s)O(1/\sqrt{s}) to O⁡(1/s)O(1/s). Thus, when there is no abandonment (i.e., θmax=0\theta_{\max}=0), Theorem 1 yields O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) time-average regret, or equivalently, O⁡(1)O(1) cumulative regret.

For comparison, Aveklouris et al. (2025) develop matching-rate-based and priority-ordering policies in a similar high-volume regime. Both policies make matching decisions only at scheduled review times, with intervals proportional to s−2/3s^{-2/3}. Let πr\pi^{\mathrm{r}} denote either policy. Expressed in our approximation-ratio notation, their results imply

limT→∞lims→∞ρT,sπr=1.\lim_{T\to\infty}\lim_{s\to\infty}\rho_{T,s}^{\pi^{\mathrm{r}}}=1.

Their proof first takes s→∞s\to\infty, so that the large number of arrivals within each review period yields a fluid approximation of the system. Then T→∞T\to\infty is taken so that the fluid queues approach the invariant queue lengths specified by their optimal fluid benchmark.

In contrast, Corollary 1 and Proposition 1 provide explicit approximation guarantees at every market size s≥1s\geq 1 and horizon T≥1T\geq 1, without taking either limit.

5 Analysis of the Longest-Queue Policy

In this section, we prove Theorem 1 for the longest-queue policy defined in Algorithm 1. We first introduce a restricted inner product and norms that will be used throughout the rest of the paper. For vectors u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, write

⟨u,v⟩ℐ+≔∑i∈ℐ+ui​vi\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}u_{i}v_{i}

and

‖u‖ℐ+≔(∑i∈ℐ+ui2)1/2,‖u‖1,ℐ+≔∑i∈ℐ+|ui|\|u\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\coloneqq\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}u_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2},\qquad\|u\|_{1,\mathcal{I}^{+}}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}|u_{i}|

for the corresponding ℓ2\ell_{2}- and ℓ1\ell_{1}-norms. Unless otherwise specified, ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} denotes the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm, and ‖u‖∞≔maxi⁡|ui|\|u\|_{\infty}\coloneqq\max_{i}|u_{i}| the maximum norm.

The proof proceeds in four steps. First, in Section 5.1, we express the regret T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] in terms of the queue lengths of the critical agents, qi​(t)q_{i}(t) for i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}. Second, in Section 5.2, we establish a negative-drift condition for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\left\|q(t)\right\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. Third, in Section 5.3, we use this drift condition to obtain a bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\left\|q(t)\right\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}] that is uniform in the time tt and in the scale ss. Finally, in Section 5.4, we substitute this queue bound into the regret representation to prove Theorem 1.

5.1 Bounding Regret Using Critical Queue Lengths

In this subsection, we express regret in terms of the critical queue lengths. First, although the objective nets matching rewards against holding and abandonment costs, Lemma 2 shows that the regret T⋅F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]T\cdot F^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] reduces to a gap in adjusted reward. Specifically, it equals the difference between the fluid benchmark’s cumulative adjusted reward T​⟨r~,x∗⟩T\langle\widetilde{r},x^{*}\rangle and the policy’s expected cumulative adjusted reward 𝔼⁡[∑mr~m​Xmπ​(T)]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{m}\widetilde{r}_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)].

Lemma 2.

For any admissible policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, the regret satisfies

T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]=T⁡⟨r~,x∗⟩−𝔼⁡[∑m=1dr~m​Xmπ​(T)],\displaystyle TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]=T\langle\widetilde{r},x^{*}\rangle-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}\widetilde{r}_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right],

where the adjusted reward r~m\widetilde{r}_{m} is defined in (8).

The proof of Lemma 2 is deferred to Appendix B.1.1. For the remainder of the analysis, we focus on our longest-queue policy π=πLQ\pi=\pi^{\mathrm{LQ}}, so we suppress the superscript π\pi on the processes Xπ​(t)X^{\pi}(t), Bπ​(t)B^{\pi}(t), and qπ​(t)q^{\pi}(t) for notational simplicity. With a slight abuse of notation, θ​q\theta q denotes the element-wise product (θ1​q1,…,θn​qn)(\theta_{1}q_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}q_{n}), and similarly for θ​q​(t)\theta q(t) and θ​q∗\theta q^{*}.

Proposition 2.

Under the longest-queue policy π\pi, the regret satisfies

T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =⟨U∗,𝔼⁡[q⁡(T)]⟩ℐ++∫0T𝔼⁡[⟨U∗,θ​q​(t)⟩ℐ+]​𝑑t.\displaystyle=\langle U^{*},\mathbb{E}[q(T)]\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle U^{*},\theta q(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right]dt. (19)
Proof.

By Lemma 2, the regret satisfies

T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =⟨r~,T​x∗−𝔼⁡[X⁡(T)]⟩\displaystyle=\langle\widetilde{r},Tx^{*}-\mathbb{E}\left[X(T)\right]\rangle
=⟨M⊤​U∗,T​x∗−𝔼⁡[X⁡(T)]⟩=⟨U∗,T​M​x∗−𝔼⁡[M​X​(T)]⟩,\displaystyle=\langle M^{\top}U^{*},Tx^{*}-\mathbb{E}\left[X(T)\right]\rangle=\langle U^{*},TMx^{*}-\mathbb{E}\left[MX(T)\right]\rangle, (20)

where the second equality holds as follows. For m∉ℳgm\notin\mathcal{M}^{g}, we have (M⊤​U∗)m>r~m(M^{\top}U^{*})_{m}>\widetilde{r}_{m}. Complementary slackness for (9) and (10) gives xm∗=0x^{*}_{m}=0, and our policy restricts match selection to the good matches ℳg\mathcal{M}^{g}, so Xm​(T)=0X_{m}(T)=0, hence the mm-th component of T​x∗−𝔼⁡[X⁡(T)]Tx^{*}-\mathbb{E}[X(T)] vanishes. For m∈ℳgm\in\mathcal{M}^{g}, (M⊤​U∗)m=r~m(M^{\top}U^{*})_{m}=\widetilde{r}_{m} by the definition of ℳg\mathcal{M}^{g} in (12). Replacing r~\widetilde{r} by M⊤​U∗M^{\top}U^{*} thus leaves the inner product unchanged.

Now, taking expectations in the flow-balance equation (1) and using the abandonment identity (see (31) in the proof of Lemma 1 in Appendix A)

𝔼⁡[B⁡(T)]=∫0T𝔼⁡[θ​q​(t)]​𝑑t,\mathbb{E}[B(T)]=\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\theta q(t)]\,dt,

together with 𝔼⁡[A⁡(T)]=λ​T\mathbb{E}[A(T)]=\lambda T for the Poisson arrivals, we have

𝔼⁡[M​X​(T)]=𝔼⁡[A⁡(T)−B⁡(T)−q⁡(T)]=λ​T−∫0T𝔼⁡[θ​q​(t)]​𝑑t−𝔼⁡[q⁡(T)].\mathbb{E}[MX(T)]=\mathbb{E}[A(T)-B(T)-q(T)]=\lambda T-\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\theta q(t)]\,dt-\mathbb{E}[q(T)]. (21)

T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =⟨U∗,∫0T𝔼⁡[θ​q​(t)]​𝑑t−θ​q∗​T+𝔼⁡[q⁡(T)]⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle U^{*},\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\theta q(t)\right]dt-\theta q^{*}T+\mathbb{E}\left[q(T)\right]\right\rangle

=⟨U∗,∫0T𝔼⁡[θ​q​(t)]​𝑑t⟩ℐ++⟨U∗,𝔼⁡[q⁡(T)]⟩ℐ+,\displaystyle=\left\langle U^{*},\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\theta q(t)\right]dt\right\rangle_{{\mathcal{I}}^{+}}+\left\langle U^{*},\mathbb{E}\left[q(T)\right]\right\rangle_{{\mathcal{I}}^{+}},

5.2 Negative Drift Analysis of ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\left\|{q(t)}\right\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}

Since the regret can be expressed in terms of the critical queue lengths by (19) of Proposition 2, bounding regret reduces to bounding 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}]. To obtain such a bound, we first establish a negative drift condition for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. We begin by defining the infinitesimal generator, which characterizes the instantaneous evolution of a continuous-time Markov chain.

Definition 5 (Infinitesimal Generator).

Let 𝐘\mathbf{Y} be a state space and let {Y⁡(t)}t≥0\{Y(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain on 𝐘\mathbf{Y}. Following (Bujorianu, 2012, Section 2.4.1), the infinitesimal generator ℒ\mathcal{L} acting on a bounded measurable function ff is defined by

ℒ​f​(y):=limt↓0𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y⁡(t))∣Y⁡(0)=y]−f⁡(y)t,y∈𝐘,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}f(y):=\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(Y(t))\mid Y(0)=y]-f(y)}{t},\quad y\in\mathbf{Y},

whenever this limit exists.

We now state the main result of this subsection, which establishes a negative drift condition for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2} under the GPG condition. To display the dependence on the scale ss explicitly, we write λs=s​λb\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b} in place of the general arrival-rate vector λ\lambda throughout the following analysis.

Proposition 3.

Assume that λb\lambda^{b} satisfies the GPG condition with ϵ\epsilon. Under the longest-queue policy described in Algorithm 1, given q⁡(t)q(t), we have

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2≤2​s​(−ϵn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+)+s.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 2s\left(-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right)+s.

We prove Proposition 3 by adapting the Lyapunov-drift argument of Kerimov et al. (2025), with three modifications. First, their model has no abandonment and evolves in discrete time, whereas our drift is computed through the infinitesimal generator of a continuous-time process; abandonment contributes an additional state-dependent term, which we show is nonpositive. Second, our critical types ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} and good matches ℳg\mathcal{M}^{g} are defined through an optimal dual solution U∗U^{*}, whereas their corresponding sets are identified from a unique nondegenerate primal solution. Third, they remove noncritical agents that are not matched immediately, so the corresponding queues are identically zero. We retain these agents and must account for their presence when analyzing the drift of the critical queues.

We begin by introducing notation for the matching decisions. At an arrival epoch, the policy selects a decision x⁡(t)∈{0,1}dx(t)\in\{0,1\}^{d} with at most one nonzero entry. Conditional on a type-ii arrival, we write xi​(t)x^{i}(t) for this decision, which is deterministic given q⁡(t)q(t). We define the aggregate matching rates

x¯​(t)≔∑i=1nλis​xi​(t),x¯b​(t)≔∑i=1nλib​xi​(t),\overline{x}(t)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}x^{i}(t),\qquad\overline{x}^{b}(t)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{b}x^{i}(t), (22)

so that x¯​(t)=s​x¯b​(t)\overline{x}(t)=s\overline{x}^{b}(t) under the high-volume scaling (7).

As the first step in proving Proposition 3, we calculate the infinitesimal generator acting on ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2} and obtain the following bound in terms of the aggregate matching rate x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t).

Lemma 3.

Under the longest-queue policy described in Algorithm 1, given q⁡(t)q(t), we have

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2≤2​s​⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ++s.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 2s\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+s.

The proof of Lemma 3 is deferred to Appendix B.2.1.

The bound in Lemma 3 reduces the proof of Proposition 3 to showing that

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ+≤−εn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+.\displaystyle\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. (23)

We introduce some notation. With a slight abuse of notation, we write (i,j)(i,j) for the match mm between types ii and jj. Let

𝒬+​(t):={i∈𝒩:qi​(t)>0}\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t):=\{i\in\mathcal{N}:q_{i}(t)>0\}

denote the set of agent types with positive queue length at time tt. Define

ℳ+​(t):={m=(i,j)∈ℳg:{i,j}∩𝒬+​(t)≠∅}\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{+}(t):=\{m=(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}:\{i,j\}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)\neq\emptyset\}

as the set of good matches involving at least one type with a positive queue.

We prove inequality (23) in two steps using an auxiliary variable ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t), where

𝒳⁡(t):={x∈ℝ+d:xm=0​ for all ​m∉ℳ+​(t)​ and(M​x)i≤λib​ for all ​i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)}.\mathcal{X}(t):=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}:\begin{array}[]{l}x_{m}=0\text{ for all }m\notin\mathcal{M}^{+}(t)\text{ and}\\[2.15277pt] (Mx)_{i}\leq\lambda_{i}^{b}\text{ for all }i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)\end{array}\right\}. (24)

First, we establish that x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) maximizes ⟨q⁡(t),M​x⟩ℐ+\langle q(t),Mx\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} over the feasible set 𝒳⁡(t)\mathcal{X}(t), which implies that

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ+≤⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​ξ⟩ℐ+\displaystyle\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}

for any feasible auxiliary vector ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t). This optimality result is established in Lemma 4.

Lemma 4.

Under the longest-queue policy described in Algorithm 1, x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) is an optimal solution of the following problem:

maxx∈𝒳⁡(t)⁡⟨q⁡(t),M​x⟩ℐ+,\displaystyle\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}(t)}\langle q(t),Mx\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}, (25)

where 𝒳⁡(t)\mathcal{X}(t) is defined in (24).

The proof of Lemma 4 is deferred to Appendix B.2.2. Second, we use the GPG assumption to construct a feasible auxiliary vector ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t) satisfying

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​ξ⟩ℐ+≤−εn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+.\displaystyle\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}.

The existence of such a vector is established in Lemma 5.

Lemma 5.

Assume that λb\lambda^{b} satisfies the GPG condition with ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Then there exists ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t) such that

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​ξ⟩ℐ+≤−ϵn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+.\displaystyle\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. (26)

The proof of Lemma 5 is deferred to Appendix B.2.3. We now combine the preceding bounds to complete the proof of Proposition 3.

Proof of Proposition 3.

Choose ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t) as in Lemma 5. By Lemmas 3 and 4,

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2} ≤2​s​⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ++s\displaystyle\leq 2s\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+s
≤2​s​⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​ξ⟩ℐ++s\displaystyle\leq 2s\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+s
≤−2​s​ϵn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ++s,\displaystyle\leq-\frac{2s\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+s,

where the last inequality follows from (26). ∎

5.3 Bound on ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\left\|q(t)\right\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}

Using the negative drift condition established in Section 5.2, we derive a uniform bound on the expected critical queue length 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}] for all t≥0t\geq 0, as stated in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.

Assume that λb\lambda^{b} satisfies the GPG condition with parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0. Under Algorithm 1, the expected queue length satisfies the uniform bound

𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]≤nε+(1+2​n​(2​e−3)ε)​ln⁡(2+4​nε+4​n​‖θ‖ℐ+s​ε2).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\big]\leq\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\left(1+\frac{2\sqrt{n}(2e-3)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ln\left(2+\frac{4\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{4n\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{s\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

To prove Proposition 4, we establish two properties of ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. The first is that it has bounded jumps, as stated in the following lemma.

Lemma 6.

Under Algorithm 1, the one-step change in the critical queue norm at any event time tt satisfies

|‖q⁡(t+)‖ℐ+−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+|≤1.\displaystyle\left|\|q(t+)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right|\leq 1.

The proof of Lemma 6 follows from a direct check of the change in ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} at each arrival or abandonment. The details are provided in Appendix B.3.1.

The second property is that ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} has negative drift when it is sufficiently large, as stated in the following lemma.

Lemma 7.

Assume that λb\lambda^{b} satisfies the GPG condition with parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0. Under Algorithm 1, the generator of ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} satisfies

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≤{−s​ε2​nif ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≥nε,s+n​‖θ‖ℐ+εif ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+<nε.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq\begin{cases}-\dfrac{s\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}}&\text{if }\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\geq\dfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon},\\[10.0pt] s+\dfrac{\sqrt{n}\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{\varepsilon}&\text{if }\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}<\dfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}.\end{cases}

The proof of Lemma 7 uses the squared-norm drift bound in Proposition 3, with the full derivation given in Appendix B.3.2.

Having established bounded jumps and a negative drift condition for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} in Lemmas 6 and 7, respectively, we next derive a uniform bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}]. To obtain this bound, we first establish a general result for continuous-time Markov jump processes in Lemma 8 below.

Lemma 8.

Let {Y⁡(t)}t≥0\{Y(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a continuous-time Markov process on a state space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} with jump types 𝒥\mathcal{J}, where λj​(y)\lambda_{j}(y) denotes the rate of jump j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} from state yy and Δj​(y)\Delta_{j}(y) the associated change in the state, so that a jump of type jj moves the process from yy to y+Δj​(y)y+\Delta_{j}(y). For a real-valued function ff on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, write Δj​f​(y):=f⁡(y+Δj​(y))−f⁡(y)\Delta_{j}f(y):=f(y+\Delta_{j}(y))-f(y) for the change in ff produced by such a jump. Assume the following conditions hold:

  1. 1.

    Jump representation: the generator of Definition 5 satisfies

    ℒ​φ​(y)=∑j∈𝒥λj​(y)​Δj​φ​(y)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\varphi(y)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\lambda_{j}(y)\Delta_{j}\varphi(y)

    for φ=f\varphi=f and for φ=eα​f\varphi=e^{\alpha f} with α>0\alpha>0.

  2. 2.

    Drift condition: There exist constants δ>0\delta>0, D≥0D\geq 0, and B≥0B\geq 0 such that

    ℒ​f​(y)≤−δif ​f​(y)≥D,andℒ​f​(y)≤Bif ​f​(y)<D.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}f(y)\leq-\delta\quad\text{if }f(y)\geq D,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{L}f(y)\leq B\quad\text{if }f(y)<D.
  3. 3.

    Bounded jump size: |Δj​f​(y)|≤K|\Delta_{j}f(y)|\leq K for all j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} and y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}.

  4. 4.

    Bounded upward rate: The aggregate rate of positive jumps satisfies

    ∑j∈𝒥+​(y)λj​(y)≤Λ,\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{+}(y)}\lambda_{j}(y)\leq\Lambda,

    where 𝒥+​(y)={j∈𝒥:Δj​f​(y)>0}\mathcal{J}^{+}(y)=\{j\in\mathcal{J}:\Delta_{j}f(y)>0\}.

Then for any t≥0t\geq 0, we have

𝔼⁡[f⁡(Yt)]≤1α∗​max⁡{α∗​f​(Y0),ln⁡B+δδ−α∗​C1+α∗​D},\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f(Y_{t})]\leq\frac{1}{\alpha^{*}}\max\left\{\alpha^{*}f(Y_{0}),\,\ln\frac{B+\delta}{\delta-\alpha^{*}C_{1}}+\alpha^{*}D\right\}, (27)

where C1=K​δ2+(e−32)​Λ​K2C_{1}=\frac{K\delta}{2}+(e-\frac{3}{2})\Lambda K^{2}, α∗=min⁡(1K,δ2​C1)\alpha^{*}=\min\left(\frac{1}{K},\frac{\delta}{2C_{1}}\right) and Y0=Y⁡(0)Y_{0}=Y(0) is the deterministic initial state of the process.

We outline the proof idea of Lemma 8 below, with the full proof provided in Appendix B.3.3. Following Hajek (1982), our proof uses quadratic bounds on exponential increments to convert negative drift of a function ff into negative drift of eα​fe^{\alpha f}. We adapt this argument to the continuous-time generator while allowing the aggregate downward jump rate to be unbounded. For downward jumps, bounded jump size permits the quadratic remainder to be absorbed into the negative first-order contribution, so no bound on their aggregate rate is needed. For upward jumps, the quadratic remainder is controlled by assuming that their aggregate rate is bounded. Choosing α>0\alpha>0 sufficiently small then yields negative drift of the exponential Lyapunov function outside a bounded region and, consequently, a uniform exponential-moment bound. Jensen’s inequality then gives the desired uniform bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}].

We now apply Lemma 8 to ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} to prove Proposition 4.

Proof of Proposition 4.

We apply Lemma 8 with Y⁡(t)=q⁡(t)Y(t)=q(t) and f⁡(q)=‖q‖ℐ+f(q)=\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. The jump types are arrivals (type ii, rate λis\lambda_{i}^{s}) and abandonments (type i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}, rate θi​qi\theta_{i}q_{i}), with corresponding changes

Δarr,i​f​(q)=‖q+ei−M​xi‖ℐ+−‖q‖ℐ+,Δabd,i​f​(q)=‖q−ei‖ℐ+−‖q‖ℐ+.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{arr},i}f(q)=\|q+e_{i}-Mx^{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}},\qquad\Delta_{\mathrm{abd},i}f(q)=\|q-e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}.

First, we verify the conditions of Lemma 8. Condition 1 is the generator formula for the queue process q⁡(t)q(t), applied to ff and eα​fe^{\alpha f} (see Lemma 9). Condition 2 holds by Lemma 7, with

δ=s​ε2​n,D=nε,B=s+n​‖θ‖ℐ+ε.\displaystyle\delta=\frac{s\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}},\qquad D=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon},\qquad B=s+\frac{\sqrt{n}\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{\varepsilon}.

Condition 3 holds with K=1K=1 by Lemma 6, and Condition 4 holds with Λ=s\Lambda=s, since only arrivals can increase ‖q‖ℐ+\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} and the total arrival rate is ∑i=1nλis=s\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}=s.

Next, we compute the constant C1C_{1}. Substituting the values above, we obtain

C1=K​δ2+(e−32)​Λ​K2=s​ε4​n+s⁡(e−32).\displaystyle C_{1}=\frac{K\delta}{2}+(e-\frac{3}{2})\Lambda K^{2}=\frac{s\varepsilon}{4\sqrt{n}}+s(e-\frac{3}{2}).

To determine α∗=min⁡(1K,δ2​C1)\alpha^{*}=\min\left(\frac{1}{K},\frac{\delta}{2C_{1}}\right), we compute

δ2​C1=s​ε2​ns​ε2​n+2​s​(e−32)<1=1K,\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{2C_{1}}=\frac{\frac{s\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}}}{\frac{s\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}}+2s(e-\frac{3}{2})}<1=\frac{1}{K},

so α∗=δ2​C1\alpha^{*}=\frac{\delta}{2C_{1}}. The inverse of α∗\alpha^{*} simplifies to

1α∗=2​C1δ=1+2​n​(2​e−3)ε.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\alpha^{*}}=\frac{2C_{1}}{\delta}=1+\frac{2\sqrt{n}(2e-3)}{\varepsilon}.

Since α∗​C1=δ2\alpha^{*}C_{1}=\frac{\delta}{2}, the logarithmic term in (27) simplifies to

B+δδ−α∗​C1=B+δδ/2=2​(Bδ+1)=2+4​nε+4​n​‖θ‖ℐ+s​ε2.\displaystyle\frac{B+\delta}{\delta-\alpha^{*}C_{1}}=\frac{B+\delta}{\delta/2}=2\left(\frac{B}{\delta}+1\right)=2+\frac{4\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{4n\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{s\varepsilon^{2}}.

Since q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0, the bound (27) from Lemma 8 yields

𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]≤nε+(1+2​n​(2​e−3)ε)​ln⁡(2+4​nε+4​n​‖θ‖ℐ+s​ε2).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr]\leq\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\left(1+\frac{2\sqrt{n}(2e-3)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ln\left(2+\frac{4\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{4n\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{s\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

5.4 Proof of the Main Result

We now combine the regret representation in Proposition 2 and the uniform queue bound in Proposition 4 to prove Theorem 1. The GPG condition enters through the negative-drift argument underlying Proposition 4.

Proof of Theorem 1.

Consider the system with arrival-rate vector λs=s​λb\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b}, writing Fs∗F_{s}^{*}, Fsπ​(T)F_{s}^{\pi}(T), and ℬq​(s)\mathcal{B}_{q}(s) for the corresponding quantities. The nonnegativity of the regret follows from the fluid upper bound in Lemma 1. For the upper bound, by Proposition 2, we have

T​Fs∗−𝔼⁡[Fsπ​(T)]=⟨U∗,𝔼⁡[q⁡(T)]⟩ℐ++∫0T𝔼⁡[⟨U∗,θ​q​(t)⟩ℐ+]​𝑑t.\displaystyle TF_{s}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)]=\langle U^{*},\mathbb{E}[q(T)]\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle U^{*},\theta q(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right]{\rm d}t.

Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to each term yields

T​Fs∗−𝔼⁡[Fsπ​(T)]\displaystyle TF_{s}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F_{s}^{\pi}(T)] ≤‖U∗‖ℐ+​𝔼​[‖q⁡(T)‖ℐ+]+∫0T‖θ‖∞​‖U∗‖ℐ+​𝔼​[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\|U^{*}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|q(T)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr]+\int_{0}^{T}\|\theta\|_{\infty}\|U^{*}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr]{\rm d}t
≤n​r~max​ℬq​(s)+T​‖θ‖∞​n​r~max​ℬq​(s),\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}\,\mathcal{B}_{q}(s)+T\|\theta\|_{\infty}\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}\,\mathcal{B}_{q}(s),

where the second inequality follows from the dual bound ‖U∗‖ℐ+≤n​r~max\|U^{*}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max} of Lemma 11 in Appendix B.4, together with the uniform queue bound 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]≤ℬq​(s)\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}]\leq\mathcal{B}_{q}(s) for all t≥0t\geq 0, established in Proposition 4, with

6 Numerical Results

In this section, we numerically evaluate our longest-queue policy against two benchmarks from Aveklouris et al. (2025): the matching-rate-based policy and the priority ordering policy. Both benchmarks are discrete-review policies that make matches only at review times, with review period ℓs=ℓs−2/3\ell_{s}=\ell s^{-2/3} for a constant ℓ>0\ell>0. The matching-rate-based policy tracks the optimal matching rates of the fluid LP as closely as agent availability allows. The priority ordering policy constructs a fixed ordering of match types based on an optimal extreme-point solution of the fluid LP and greedily makes matches in that order at each review time, subject to agent availability.

We consider three instances of the dynamic matching problem with abandonment. For each instance, we vary the market scale over s∈{10,20,…,200}s\in\{10,20,\ldots,200\}. At each scale, we simulate 100100 independent replications over a fixed time horizon T=100T=100 to estimate each policy’s approximation ratio. We then compare these ratios to assess how policy performance changes as ss increases.

For these comparisons, we use three review periods for the benchmark policies: ℓs=s−2/3\ell_{s}=s^{-2/3}, ℓs=0.1\ell_{s}=0.1, and ℓs=0.3\ell_{s}=0.3. The first follows the review rule proposed in Aveklouris et al. (2025), while the two fixed periods are also used in their numerical experiments. Our longest-queue policy acts at arrival epochs and requires no review interval, so its performance is unchanged across these choices of review period.

We begin with two bipartite matching instances each with four demand types, D1,…,D4D_{1},\ldots,D_{4}, and four supply types, S1,…,S4S_{1},\ldots,S_{4}. The first instance follows the numerical setting in Section 6.1 of Aveklouris et al. (2025), with exponential patience times of the same mean and an additional abandonment cost. The demand and supply arrival-rate vectors are (3,2,1,3)(3,2,1,3) and (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2), respectively. For each demand type DiD_{i}, let vi=(rDi​S1,rDi​S2,rDi​S3,rDi​S4)v_{i}=(r_{D_{i}S_{1}},r_{D_{i}S_{2}},r_{D_{i}S_{3}},r_{D_{i}S_{4}}) denote its matching-reward vector. We set v1=(1,2,3,1)v_{1}=(1,2,3,1), v2=(1,1,1,1)v_{2}=(1,1,1,1), v3=(2,1,1,2)v_{3}=(2,1,1,2), and v4=(3,3,2,1)v_{4}=(3,3,2,1). The holding-cost rates are (cD1,cD2,cD3,cD4)=(1,2,1,2)(c_{D_{1}},c_{D_{2}},c_{D_{3}},c_{D_{4}})=(1,2,1,2) and (cS1,cS2,cS3,cS4)=(2,1,2,1)(c_{S_{1}},c_{S_{2}},c_{S_{3}},c_{S_{4}})=(2,1,2,1). For every agent type kk, the abandonment rate is θk=3\theta_{k}=3, corresponding to a mean patience time of 1/31/3, and the abandonment cost is γk=1/5\gamma_{k}=1/5. We also include the terminal cost specified in (2).

Under this parameter setting, the fluid LP has multiple optimal dual solutions, so the first instance violates the GPG condition. For the second instance, we increase only the arrival rate of D1D_{1} from 33 to 44, keeping all other parameters unchanged. With this change, the optimal fluid dual solution is unique and hence the GPG condition holds, i.e., the fluid has a positive GPG.

In both instances shown in Figures 1 and 2, our longest-queue policy achieves a higher approximation ratio than the two benchmark policies for every tested scale ss and all three review periods ℓs\ell_{s}. The approximation ratio of our policy approaches 11 more rapidly, especially in the second instance, where the GPG is positive (Figure 2). Both benchmark policies perform worse with longer review periods, as seen when the fixed interval increases from 0.10.1 to 0.30.3. This is expected because agents may abandon during the longer wait for the next review, leading to lost matching opportunities. Our longest-queue policy instead makes matching decisions at arrival epochs, using a rule that restricts attention to good matches and gives priority to critical agent types. It therefore avoids this additional costly delay and outperforms both benchmark policies in these experiments.

To further compare the policies’ convergence rates, we plot log⁡(1−ρ⁡(s))\log(1-\rho(s)) against log⁡s\log s in Figure 3, where ρ⁡(s)\rho(s) denotes the approximation ratio. For this comparison, we use ℓs=s−2/3\ell_{s}=s^{-2/3} for the two benchmark policies, as this choice yields their best performance at larger market scales. When 1−ρ⁡(s)≈C​s−α1-\rho(s)\approx Cs^{-\alpha} with C,α>0C,\alpha>0, taking logarithms gives

log⁡(1−ρ⁡(s))≈log⁡C−α​log​s.\log\bigl(1-\rho(s)\bigr)\approx\log C-\alpha\log s.

The slope −α-\alpha therefore reflects the convergence rate.

In both instances, our longest-queue policy has the most negative fitted slope, indicating the fastest convergence rate among the three policies over the tested scales. In the second instance, where the GPG condition holds, its fitted slope is very close to −1-1, consistent with the O⁡(1/s)O(1/s) bound in Corollary 1. In the first instance, where GPG fails, the fitted slope is close to −0.5-0.5, consistent with the O⁡(1/s)O(1/\sqrt{s}) bound in Proposition 1.

In the third instance, we consider a non-bipartite two-way matching model with ten agent types and 24 compatible pairs. The compatibility graph contains a triangle on types 1,2,31,2,3 and is therefore non-bipartite. The base arrival-rate vector is (7,5,5,3,3,6,2,1,1,3)(7,5,5,3,3,6,2,1,1,3). For every type ii, the holding-cost rate is ci=1c_{i}=1, the abandonment rate is θi=3\theta_{i}=3, and the abandonment cost is γi=1/5\gamma_{i}=1/5. Patience times are exponentially distributed with mean 1/31/3. The rewards for the compatible matching pairs are

ri​jCompatible pairs ​{i,j}1{1,7},{4,5},{5,6}2{1,8},{6,10}3{1,2},{2,6},{4,7},{4,8},{7,9},{8,10},{9,10}4{1,3},{2,4},{2,7},{5,9},{6,9},{7,8}5{2,3},{2,5},{3,5},{3,6},{3,9},{5,8}\begin{array}[]{c|l}r_{ij}&\text{Compatible pairs }\{i,j\}\\ \hline\cr 1&\{1,7\},\ \{4,5\},\ \{5,6\}\\ 2&\{1,8\},\ \{6,10\}\\ 3&\{1,2\},\ \{2,6\},\ \{4,7\},\ \{4,8\},\ \{7,9\},\ \{8,10\},\ \{9,10\}\\ 4&\{1,3\},\ \{2,4\},\ \{2,7\},\ \{5,9\},\ \{6,9\},\ \{7,8\}\\ 5&\{2,3\},\ \{2,5\},\ \{3,5\},\ \{3,6\},\ \{3,9\},\ \{5,8\}\end{array}

Pairs not listed above are incompatible. We note that this instance satisfies the GPG condition. Moreover, while the matching network is non-bipartite, the positive-flow support of the selected optimal extreme-point solution to the fluid LP is acyclic, which allows us to construct the priority sets following Aveklouris et al. (2025) and apply the priority ordering policy.

Figure 4 shows that our longest-queue policy achieves a considerably higher approximation ratio than the two benchmark policies across all tested scales ss and review periods ℓs\ell_{s}. Its approximation ratio also approaches 11 more rapidly than those of the two benchmark policies. Thus, the performance advantage observed in the bipartite instances also appears in this non-bipartite two-way matching network.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we propose a longest-queue policy for dynamic two-way matching with abandonment. Our analysis provides explicit approximation-ratio guarantees for every s≥1s\geq 1 and T≥1T\geq 1. Under exponential patience times, we prove that our policy achieves an approximation ratio of at least 1−C1/s1-C_{1}/s under GPG and at least 1−C2/s1-C_{2}/\sqrt{s} without GPG, where C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are independent of ss and TT. The numerical experiments demonstrate that our simple longest-queue policy outperforms the existing benchmark policies. The fitted slopes of the log–log plots show that the numerical performance of our policy is consistent with our theoretical bounds.

8 Methods

Google Gemini 3 Pro was used through iterative interactions to help develop an initial proof argument for Lemma 8. The authors subsequently checked and formalized the argument, and wrote the proof presented in this paper. OpenAI GPT and Anthropic Claude models were used to assist in writing the simulation code for the numerical studies in Section 6. The authors reviewed and tested the resulting code and verified the reported numerical results.

Appendix A Fluid Upper Bound

We provide the proof of Lemma 1 by constructing a feasible solution to the fluid relaxation whose objective value equals the policy’s expected net value per unit time.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Proof of Lemma 1.

Taking expectations in the flow balance equation (1) and dividing by TT yields

∑m=1dMi​m​𝔼​[Xmπ​(T)]T+𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T+𝔼​[Biπ​(T)]T=𝔼​[Ai​(T)]T.\frac{\sum_{m=1}^{d}M_{im}\mathbb{E}[X_{m}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[A_{i}(T)]}{T}. (28)

Since arrivals of type ii follow a Poisson process with rate λi\lambda_{i},

𝔼​[Ai​(T)]T=λi.\frac{\mathbb{E}[A_{i}(T)]}{T}=\lambda_{i}. (29)

For each i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N}, each waiting type-ii agent abandons according to an independent exponential clock of rate θi\theta_{i}. The type-ii abandonment intensity at time tt is therefore the number of waiting type-ii agents times the individual abandonment rate, namely θi​qiπ​(t)\theta_{i}q_{i}^{\pi}(t). Let YiY_{i} denote a unit-rate Poisson process independent of the arrival processes and of the other primitive processes. Then the cumulative number of type-ii abandonments admits the random-time-change representation

Biπ​(t)=Yi​(θi​∫0tqiπ​(s)​𝑑s),t≥0.B_{i}^{\pi}(t)=Y_{i}\!\left(\theta_{i}\int_{0}^{t}q_{i}^{\pi}(s)\,ds\right),\qquad t\geq 0.

The same construction for type-dependent exponential abandonments is used in (Atar et al., 2004, Section 2.1, equation (4)).

By (Pang et al., 2007, Section 3.4, Lemma 3.2), the compensated time-changed process

MiB​(t)≔Biπ​(t)−θi​∫0tqiπ​(s)​𝑑sM_{i}^{B}(t)\coloneqq B_{i}^{\pi}(t)-\theta_{i}\int_{0}^{t}q_{i}^{\pi}(s)\,ds (30)

is a martingale. Since MiB​(0)=0M_{i}^{B}(0)=0, we have 𝔼⁡[MiB​(T)]=0\mathbb{E}[M_{i}^{B}(T)]=0, and taking expectations in (30) gives

𝔼⁡[Biπ​(T)]=θi​𝔼​[∫0Tqiπ​(t)​𝑑t]=θi​∫0T𝔼⁡[qiπ​(t)]​𝑑t,\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]=\theta_{i}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}q_{i}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right]=\theta_{i}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(t)]\,dt, (31)

where the last equality follows from Fubini–Tonelli’s theorem (Folland, 1999, Section 2.5, Theorem 2.37), using qiπ≥0q_{i}^{\pi}\geq 0.

Define the time-averaged queue length and matching rates as

q¯i≜1T​∫0T𝔼⁡[qiπ​(t)]​𝑑t+𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T​θi,x¯m≜𝔼​[Xmπ​(T)]T.\overline{q}_{i}\triangleq\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(t)]\,dt+\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T\theta_{i}},\qquad\overline{x}_{m}\triangleq\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_{m}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}. (32)

Combining (31) with (32), we have

θi​q¯i=𝔼​[Biπ​(T)]T+𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T.\theta_{i}\overline{q}_{i}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}. (33)

Substituting (29), (32), and (33) into (28) gives

[M​x¯]i+θi​q¯i=λi,[M\overline{x}]_{i}+\theta_{i}\overline{q}_{i}=\lambda_{i},

which is the equality constraint in (6). Since x¯m,q¯i≥0\overline{x}_{m},\overline{q}_{i}\geq 0 by construction, the pair (x¯,q¯)(\overline{x},\overline{q}) is feasible for (6).

It remains to show that 𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]/T\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]/T equals the objective of (6) evaluated at (x¯,q¯)(\overline{x},\overline{q}). Taking expectations of Fπ​(T)F^{\pi}(T) as defined in (2) and dividing by TT, we have

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]T\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]}{T} =∑m=1drm𝔼​[Xmπ​(T)]T−∑i=1nci⋅1T∫0T𝔼[qiπ(t)]dt\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_{m}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(t)]\,dt
−∑i=1nγi𝔼​[Biπ​(T)]T−∑i=1n(ciθi+γi)𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{c_{i}}{\theta_{i}}+\gamma_{i}\right)\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}
=∑m=1drm​x¯m−∑i=1nci​(1T​∫0T𝔼⁡[qiπ​(t)]​dt+𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T​θi)⏟=q¯i\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}\overline{x}_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(t)]\,dt+\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T\theta_{i}}\right)}_{=\overline{q}_{i}}
−∑i=1nγi(𝔼​[Biπ​(T)]T+𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]T)⏟=θi​q¯i\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}\underbrace{\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\right)}_{=\theta_{i}\overline{q}_{i}}
=∑m=1drm​x¯m−∑i=1n(ci+θi​γi)​q¯i\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}\overline{x}_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(c_{i}+\theta_{i}\gamma_{i})\overline{q}_{i}
=∑m=1drm​x¯m−∑i=1nc¯i​q¯i,\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}\overline{x}_{m}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\overline{c}_{i}\overline{q}_{i},

where we used (32) and (33). This is exactly the objective of (6) evaluated at (x¯,q¯)(\overline{x},\overline{q}). Since F∗​(λ)F^{*}(\lambda) is the optimal value of (6), we conclude

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]T≤F∗​(λ).\frac{\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]}{T}\leq F^{*}(\lambda).

∎

B.1.1 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof of Lemma 2.

Taking expectations of Fπ​(T)F^{\pi}(T) as defined in (2) yields

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =𝔼⁡[∑m=1drm​Xmπ​(T)]−∑i=1nci​𝔼​[∫0Tqiπ​(t)​𝑑t]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}q_{i}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right]
−∑i=1nγi𝔼[Biπ(T)]−∑i=1n(ciθi+γi)𝔼[qiπ(T)].\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{c_{i}}{\theta_{i}}+\gamma_{i}\right)\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]. (34)

As established in (31), the expected cumulative number of type-ii abandonments satisfies

𝔼⁡[Biπ​(T)]=θi​𝔼​[∫0Tqiπ​(t)​𝑑t].\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{\pi}(T)]=\theta_{i}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}q_{i}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right].

Substituting this identity into the expectation of the flow-balance equation (1) and rearranging yields

𝔼⁡[∫0Tqiπ​(t)​𝑑t]=1θi​(λi​T−𝔼⁡[qiπ​(T)]−𝔼⁡[(M​Xπ​(T))i]),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}q_{i}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right]=\frac{1}{\theta_{i}}\left(\lambda_{i}T-\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]-\mathbb{E}[(MX^{\pi}(T))_{i}]\right), (35)

where we used 𝔼⁡[Ai​(T)]=λi​T\mathbb{E}[A_{i}(T)]=\lambda_{i}T since arrivals follow a Poisson process with rate λi\lambda_{i}.

Substituting (31) and (35) into (34) gives

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =𝔼⁡[∑m=1drm​Xmπ​(T)]−∑i=1nciθi​(λi​T−𝔼⁡[qiπ​(T)]−𝔼⁡[(M​Xπ​(T))i])\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{c_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\left(\lambda_{i}T-\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]-\mathbb{E}[(MX^{\pi}(T))_{i}]\right)
−∑i=1nγi(λiT−𝔼[qiπ(T)]−𝔼[(MXπ(T))i])−∑i=1n(ciθi+γi)𝔼[qiπ(T)]\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}T-\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]-\mathbb{E}[(MX^{\pi}(T))_{i}]\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{c_{i}}{\theta_{i}}+\gamma_{i}\right)\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]
=𝔼⁡[∑m=1drm​Xmπ​(T)]−∑i=1nc¯iθi​(λi​T−𝔼⁡[qiπ​(T)]−𝔼⁡[(M​Xπ​(T))i])−∑i=1nc¯iθi​𝔼​[qiπ​(T)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\left(\lambda_{i}T-\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)]-\mathbb{E}[(MX^{\pi}(T))_{i}]\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)],

where the second equality follows from the definition of c¯i\overline{c}_{i} in (5). The 𝔼​[qiπ​(T)]\mathbb{E}[q_{i}^{\pi}(T)] terms cancel, yielding

𝔼​[Fπ​(T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)] =𝔼⁡[∑m=1drm​Xmπ​(T)]+∑i=1nc¯iθi​𝔼​[(M​Xπ​(T))i]−∑i=1nc¯i​λi​Tθi\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}r_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\mathbb{E}[(MX^{\pi}(T))_{i}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}\lambda_{i}T}{\theta_{i}}
=𝔼⁡[∑m=1d(rm+∑i=1nc¯iθi​Mi​m)​Xmπ​(T)]−∑i=1nc¯i​λi​Tθi\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}\left(r_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}}{\theta_{i}}M_{im}\right)X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}\lambda_{i}T}{\theta_{i}}
=𝔼⁡[∑m=1dr~m​Xmπ​(T)]−∑i=1nc¯i​λi​Tθi,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}\widetilde{r}_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}\lambda_{i}T}{\theta_{i}},

where the last equality follows from the definition of r~m\widetilde{r}_{m} in (8). Equation (11) gives the optimal fluid objective value F∗F^{*}; multiplying it by TT gives

T​F∗=T⁡⟨r~,x∗⟩−∑i=1nc¯i​λi​Tθi.TF^{*}=T\langle\widetilde{r},x^{*}\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\overline{c}_{i}\lambda_{i}T}{\theta_{i}}.

T​F∗−𝔼⁡[Fπ​(T)]=T⁡⟨r~,x∗⟩−𝔼⁡[∑m=1dr~m​Xmπ​(T)].\displaystyle TF^{*}-\mathbb{E}[F^{\pi}(T)]=T\langle\widetilde{r},x^{*}\rangle-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^{d}\widetilde{r}_{m}X_{m}^{\pi}(T)\right].
