B.2 Proofs for Section 5.2

We provide the proofs of the auxiliary lemmas used to establish Proposition 3.

B.2.1 Proof of Lemma 3

Using Definition 5, we first derive an expression for ℒ​f​(q⁡(t))\mathcal{L}f(q(t)) under the longest-queue policy.

Lemma 9.

Under Algorithm 1, the queue length process {q⁡(t)}t≥0\{q(t)\}_{t\geq 0} evolves as a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain on ℤ+n\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n}. Given the current state q⁡(t)=qq(t)=q, the process is driven by two types of events:

  1. 1.

    Arrivals: Type-ii agents arrive as a Poisson process with rate λi\lambda_{i}, causing q→q+ei−M​xi​(t)q\to q+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t), as in (8).

  2. 2.

    Abandonments: Each agent in queue ii abandons independently at rate θi\theta_{i}, causing q→q−eiq\to q-e_{i}, as in (10).

The infinitesimal generator acting on a bounded measurable function ff is

ℒ​f​(q)=∑i=1nλi​[f⁡(q+ei−M​xi​(t))−f⁡(q)]+∑i=1nθi​qi​[f⁡(q−ei)−f⁡(q)].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}f(q)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\bigl[f(q+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t))-f(q)\bigr]+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}q_{i}\bigl[f(q-e_{i})-f(q)\bigr]. (36)
Proof of Lemma 9.

By Definition 5, the generator is ℒ​f​(q)=limh↓0𝔼⁡[f⁡(q⁡(t+h))∣q⁡(t)=q]−f⁡(q)h\mathcal{L}f(q)=\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(q(t+h))\mid q(t)=q]-f(q)}{h}. We compute this limit by analyzing the event probabilities over [t,t+h)[t,t+h). By the standard infinitesimal transition probabilities for independent Poisson arrivals and exponential abandonments, we have

ℙ(one type-i arrival in [t,t+h)∣q(t)=q)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\text{one type-}i\text{ arrival in }[t,t+h)\mid q(t)=q) =λi​h+o⁡(h),\displaystyle=\lambda_{i}h+o(h), (37)
ℙ(one type-i abandonment in [t,t+h)∣q(t)=q)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\text{one type-}i\text{ abandonment in }[t,t+h)\mid q(t)=q) =θi​qi​h+o⁡(h),\displaystyle=\theta_{i}q_{i}h+o(h),
ℙ(two or more events in [t,t+h)∣q(t)=q)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\text{two or more events in }[t,t+h)\mid q(t)=q) =o⁡(h),\displaystyle=o(h),
ℙ(no event in [t,t+h)∣q(t)=q)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\text{no event in }[t,t+h)\mid q(t)=q) =1−Λ⁡(q)​h+o⁡(h),\displaystyle=1-\Lambda(q)h+o(h),

where Λ⁡(q)=∑i=1nλi+∑i=1nθi​qi\Lambda(q)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}q_{i} is the total event rate, and g⁡(h)=o⁡(h)g(h)=o(h) means limh↓0g⁡(h)/h=0\lim_{h\downarrow 0}g(h)/h=0.

Conditioning on which event occurs and using the event probabilities (37) together with the transitions (8) and (10), we have

𝔼⁡[f⁡(q⁡(t+h))∣q⁡(t)=q]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f(q(t+h))\mid q(t)=q] =f⁡(q)​(1−Λ⁡(q)​h)+∑i=1nλi​h⋅f⁡(q+ei−M​xi​(t))\displaystyle=f(q)(1-\Lambda(q)h)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h\cdot f(q+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t))
+∑i=1nθiqih⋅f(q−ei)+o(h).\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}q_{i}h\cdot f(q-e_{i})+o(h).

Subtracting f⁡(q)f(q) and dividing by hh yields

𝔼⁡[f⁡(q⁡(t+h))∣q⁡(t)=q]−f⁡(q)h=∑i=1nλi​[f⁡(q+ei−M​xi​(t))−f⁡(q)]+∑i=1nθi​qi​[f⁡(q−ei)−f⁡(q)]+o⁡(h)h.\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(q(t+h))\mid q(t)=q]-f(q)}{h}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\bigl[f(q+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t))-f(q)\bigr]+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}q_{i}\bigl[f(q-e_{i})-f(q)\bigr]+\frac{o(h)}{h}.

Taking h↓0h\downarrow 0 yields (36). ∎

Having established the generator in Lemma 9, we now prove Lemma 3 by applying it to the squared norm of the critical queues.

Proof of Lemma 3.

Applying the generator (36) from Lemma 9 to f⁡(q)=‖q‖ℐ+2=∑i∈ℐ+qi2f(q)=\|q\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}q_{i}^{2} yields

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} =∑i∈ℐ+λis​[(qi​(t)+1−[M​xi​(t)]i)2+∑j≠i,j∈ℐ+(qj​(t)−[M​xi​(t)]j)2−∑j∈ℐ+qj​(t)2]\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left[\left(q_{i}(t)+1-[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}\right)^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i,j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\left(q_{j}(t)-[Mx^{i}(t)]_{j}\right)^{2}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}q_{j}(t)^{2}\right]
+∑i∈[n]∖ℐ+λis[∑j∈ℐ+(qj(t)−[Mxi(t)]j)2−∑j∈ℐ+qj(t)2]\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\left(q_{j}(t)-[Mx^{i}(t)]_{j}\right)^{2}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}q_{j}(t)^{2}\right]
+∑i∈ℐ+θiqi(t)[(qi(t)−1)2−qi(t)2],\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\theta_{i}q_{i}(t)\left[\left(q_{i}(t)-1\right)^{2}-q_{i}(t)^{2}\right],

where the abandonment sum is restricted to i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+} since abandonments from i∉ℐ+i\notin\mathcal{I}^{+} do not affect ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. Expanding the squared terms gives

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} =∑i∈ℐ+λis​[2​qi​(t)−2​⟨q⁡(t),M​xi​(t)⟩ℐ++1−2​[M​xi​(t)]i+‖M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2]\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left[2q_{i}(t)-2\langle q(t),Mx^{i}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+1-2[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}+\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right]
+∑i∈[n]∖ℐ+λis[−2⟨q(t),Mxi(t)⟩ℐ++∥Mxi(t)∥ℐ+2]\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left[-2\langle q(t),Mx^{i}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right]
+∑i∈ℐ+θiqi(t)[−2qi(t)+1].\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\theta_{i}q_{i}(t)\left[-2q_{i}(t)+1\right]. (38)

Since qi​(t)q_{i}(t) is a nonnegative integer, qi​(t)​[−2​qi​(t)+1]≤0q_{i}(t)\left[-2q_{i}(t)+1\right]\leq 0, so the abandonment term is non-positive and we drop it. Combining the remaining terms and substituting the definition (22) of x¯​(t)\overline{x}(t), we obtain

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2≤2​⟨q⁡(t),λs−M​x¯​(t)⟩ℐ++∑i∈ℐ+λis​(1−2​[M​xi​(t)]i)+∑i=1nλis​‖M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 2\langle q(t),\lambda^{s}-M\overline{x}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left(1-2[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. (39)

It remains to bound the last two sums. We combine them into a single sum,

∑i∈ℐ+λis​(1−2​[M​xi​(t)]i)+∑i=1nλis​‖M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2=∑i=1nλis​κi​(t),\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left(1-2[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\kappa_{i}(t),

where

κi(t)≔𝟏{i∈ℐ+}(1−2[Mxi(t)]i)+∥Mxi(t)∥ℐ+2.\displaystyle\kappa_{i}(t)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}\left(1-2[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}\right)+\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}.

We show that κi​(t)≤1\kappa_{i}(t)\leq 1 for every ii. Since M​xi​(t)Mx^{i}(t) has entries in {0,1}\{0,1\}, we have

‖M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2=∑k∈ℐ+([M​xi​(t)]k)2=∑k∈ℐ+[M​xi​(t)]k.\displaystyle\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\left([Mx^{i}(t)]_{k}\right)^{2}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}[Mx^{i}(t)]_{k}.

Upon a type-ii arrival, either no match is selected or the arriving agent is matched with exactly one waiting agent.

If no match is selected, then xi​(t)=0x^{i}(t)=0 and M​xi​(t)=0Mx^{i}(t)=0, so κi(t)=𝟏{i∈ℐ+}≤1\kappa_{i}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}\leq 1.

If a match mm with 𝒩⁡(m)={i,j}\mathcal{N}(m)=\{i,j\} is selected, then M​xi​(t)=ei+ejMx^{i}(t)=e_{i}+e_{j}, so [M​xi​(t)]i=1[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}=1 and ∥Mxi(t)∥ℐ+2=𝟏{i∈ℐ+}+𝟏{j∈ℐ+}\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}+\mathbf{1}\{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}. Hence

κi(t)=−𝟏{i∈ℐ+}+𝟏{i∈ℐ+}+𝟏{j∈ℐ+}=𝟏{j∈ℐ+}≤1.\displaystyle\kappa_{i}(t)=-\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}+\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}+\mathbf{1}\{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}=\mathbf{1}\{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}\leq 1.

In both cases κi​(t)≤1\kappa_{i}(t)\leq 1, so

∑i∈ℐ+λis​(1−2​[M​xi​(t)]i)+∑i=1nλis​‖M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2≤∑i=1nλis=‖λs‖1=s,\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left(1-2[Mx^{i}(t)]_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\|Mx^{i}(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}=\|\lambda^{s}\|_{1}=s, (40)

where the last equality uses ‖λs‖1=s​‖λb‖1=s\|\lambda^{s}\|_{1}=s\|\lambda^{b}\|_{1}=s. Combining (39) and (40), we obtain

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2≤2​s​⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ++s.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 2s\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+s.

∎

B.2.2 Proof of Lemma 4

Before proving the optimality result in Lemma 4, we first establish a simple property of our algorithm. Because the policy is maximally aggressive on good matches, no two waiting agents can ever form a good match. Whenever a new agent arrives, the algorithm immediately matches it if some waiting agent forms a good match with it. Hence if such a pair of waiting agents existed, the later arrival would have been matched on arrival, since the earlier agent was already present and available.

Lemma 10.

Under Algorithm 1, for every good match (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g} and every t≥0t\geq 0,

qi​(t)​qj​(t)=0.\displaystyle q_{i}(t)\,q_{j}(t)=0.

In particular, if i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), then 𝒩i+​(t)=𝒩i0​(t)=∅\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}(t)=\mathcal{N}^{0}_{i}(t)=\emptyset, where 𝒩i+​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t) and 𝒩i0​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{0}(t) are defined in (13) and (14), respectively.

Proof.

We prove by contradiction. Suppose that at time tt there exist types ii and jj such that qi​(t)>0q_{i}(t)>0, qj​(t)>0q_{j}(t)>0, and (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g} is a good match. Then we can pick a specific type-ii item and a specific type-jj item that are available at time tt, i.e., they have arrived but have not been matched and have not abandoned by time tt. Let tit_{i} and tjt_{j} denote their arrival times, respectively, and without loss of generality assume ti<tj≤tt_{i}<t_{j}\leq t.

Consider the system at time tjt_{j}, when this type-jj item arrives. The chosen type-ii item is already present at time tjt_{j} (because ti<tjt_{i}<t_{j}) and remains available at time tt; hence it is also available at time tjt_{j}. Since (i,j)(i,j) is a good match and the type-ii item is available, the arriving type-jj item has at least one available good neighbor. Algorithm 1 therefore matches it on arrival, possibly with a different neighbor whose queue is longer. This contradicts the assumption that the type-jj item is available at time tt. Hence qi​(t)​qj​(t)=0q_{i}(t)q_{j}(t)=0 for every (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}.

Now let i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), so that qi​(t)>0q_{i}(t)>0. For every jj with (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}, the first part gives qj​(t)=0q_{j}(t)=0. Since 𝒩i+​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t) and 𝒩i0​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{0}(t), defined in (13) and (14), respectively, both require qj​(t)>0q_{j}(t)>0 and (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}, they are empty. ∎

Building on this structural property, we now prove Lemma 4, which shows that x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) is an optimal solution of problem (25).

Proof of Lemma 4.

Let δ⁡(j):={i:Mi​m=Mj​m=1}\delta(j):=\{i:M_{im}=M_{jm}=1\} denote the set of agent types that can be matched with type jj. For any x∈𝒳⁡(t)x\in\mathcal{X}(t), we have

⟨q⁡(t),M​x⟩ℐ+\displaystyle\langle q(t),Mx\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} =∑i∈[n]∑j∈δ⁡(i)∩ℐ+qj​(t)​x(i,j)\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[n]}\sum_{j\in\delta(i)\cap\mathcal{I}^{+}}q_{j}(t)x_{(i,j)}
=∑i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)∑j∈𝒩i+​(t)qj​(t)​x(i,j).\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)}q_{j}(t)x_{(i,j)}. (41)

The last equality holds due to the following three observations:

  1. 1.

    Since qj​(t)=0q_{j}(t)=0 for j∉𝒬+​(t)j\notin\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), only terms with j∈𝒬+​(t)j\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) contribute.

  2. 2.

    The constraint xm=0x_{m}=0 for m∉ℳ+​(t)m\notin\mathcal{M}^{+}(t) leaves only good matches, so the inner index is further restricted to those jj with (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}. Together with the previous observation, the surviving indices are exactly {j∈ℐ+:qj(t)>0,(i,j)∈ℳg}=𝒩i+(t)\{j\in\mathcal{I}^{+}:q_{j}(t)>0,\ (i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}\}=\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t) by (13).

  3. 3.

    By Lemma 10, 𝒩i+​(t)=∅\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)=\emptyset for all i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), eliminating all terms with i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t).

From (41), since i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) and j∈𝒬+​(t)j\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), each variable x(i,j)x_{(i,j)} appears exactly once. Thus, problem (25) decomposes into independent subproblems, one for each i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) with 𝒩i+​(t)≠∅\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)\neq\emptyset, namely

𝒫i(t):maxx(i,j),j∈𝒩i+​(t)∑j∈𝒩i+​(t)qj​(t)​x(i,j)s.t.∑j∈𝒩i+​(t)x(i,j)≤λbi,x(i,j)≥0∀j∈𝒩i+(t).\mathcal{P}_{i}(t):\quad\begin{aligned} \max_{x_{(i,j)},\,j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)}\quad&\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)}q_{j}(t)x_{(i,j)}\\ \text{s.t.}\quad&\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t)}x_{(i,j)}\leq\lambda^{b}_{i},\quad x_{(i,j)}\geq 0\quad\forall j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t).\end{aligned} (42)

We now show that x¯b​(t)=∑i∈[n]λib​xi​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t)=\sum_{i\in[n]}\lambda^{b}_{i}x^{i}(t) is feasible for (25) and solves every subproblem.

Feasibility. We first show that x¯b​(t)∈𝒳​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t)\in\mathcal{X}(t). By Algorithm 1, matches occur only for good match types and only when the arriving agent can be matched with a compatible agent currently in the queue. For any m=(i,j)∉ℳ+​(t)m=(i,j)\notin\mathcal{M}^{+}(t), the algorithm never selects such a match, so x¯mb​(t)=0\overline{x}^{b}_{m}(t)=0.

Now fix i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), so that qi​(t)=0q_{i}(t)=0; these are the only coordinates at which 𝒳⁡(t)\mathcal{X}(t) imposes a capacity constraint. For any j∈δ⁡(i)j\in\delta(i),

x¯(i,j)b​(t)=λib​x(i,j)i​(t)+λjb​x(i,j)j​(t).\displaystyle\overline{x}^{b}_{(i,j)}(t)=\lambda^{b}_{i}x^{i}_{(i,j)}(t)+\lambda^{b}_{j}x^{j}_{(i,j)}(t).

When a type-jj agent arrives, no type-ii agent is waiting since qi​(t)=0q_{i}(t)=0, so x(i,j)j​(t)=0x^{j}_{(i,j)}(t)=0. Therefore,

x¯(i,j)b​(t)=λib​x(i,j)i​(t)for all ​j∈δ⁡(i),\displaystyle\overline{x}^{b}_{(i,j)}(t)=\lambda^{b}_{i}x^{i}_{(i,j)}(t)\quad\text{for all }j\in\delta(i), (43)

and hence

(M​x¯b​(t))i=∑j∈δ⁡(i)x¯(i,j)b​(t)=λib​∑j∈δ⁡(i)x(i,j)i​(t)≤λib,\displaystyle(M\overline{x}^{b}(t))_{i}=\sum_{j\in\delta(i)}\overline{x}^{b}_{(i,j)}(t)=\lambda^{b}_{i}\sum_{j\in\delta(i)}x^{i}_{(i,j)}(t)\leq\lambda^{b}_{i},

where the inequality holds since the algorithm selects at most one match per arrival. Thus x¯b​(t)∈𝒳​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t)\in\mathcal{X}(t).

Optimality. Consider i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) with 𝒩i+​(t)≠∅\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}(t)\neq\emptyset. By (43), the components of x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) in problem 𝒫i​(t)\mathcal{P}_{i}(t) are x¯(i,j)b​(t)=λib​x(i,j)i​(t)\overline{x}^{b}_{(i,j)}(t)=\lambda^{b}_{i}x^{i}_{(i,j)}(t), j∈𝒩i+​(t)j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t). Since the objective coefficients qj​(t)q_{j}(t) of 𝒫i​(t)\mathcal{P}_{i}(t) are nonnegative and its only constraint is the total capacity λib\lambda^{b}_{i}, 𝒫i​(t)\mathcal{P}_{i}(t) is solved by giving the entire mass λib\lambda^{b}_{i} to a longest queue in 𝒩i+​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t). This is exactly our decision rule: Algorithm 1 matches an arriving type-ii agent with the longest queue arg⁡maxj∈𝒩i+​(t)​qj​(t)\arg\max_{j\in\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}(t)}q_{j}(t), so x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) gives mass λib\lambda^{b}_{i} to this queue and zero to every other type in 𝒩i+​(t)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}(t). Thus x¯b​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t) solves every problem 𝒫i​(t)\mathcal{P}_{i}(t), and since x¯b​(t)∈𝒳​(t)\overline{x}^{b}(t)\in\mathcal{X}(t), it is optimal for (25).

∎

B.2.3 Proof of Lemma 5

Having proved Lemma 4, we now turn to Lemma 5. Its proof uses the GPG condition to construct a feasible auxiliary vector ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t) satisfying (26).

Proof of Lemma 5.

Define

λ^i​(t)={λib,if ​i∉ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t),λib+ϵ/n,if ​i∈ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t).\widehat{\lambda}_{i}(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda_{i}^{b},&\text{if }i\notin\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t),\\[4.0pt] \lambda_{i}^{b}+\epsilon/\sqrt{n},&\text{if }i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t).\end{cases}

Since |ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t)|≤n|\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)|\leq n, we have

‖λ^​(t)−λb‖2=ϵn​|ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t)|≤ϵ.\|\widehat{\lambda}(t)-\lambda^{b}\|_{2}=\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{|\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)|}\leq\epsilon.

Thus, by Definition 4, U∗U^{*} remains optimal when λb\lambda^{b} is replaced by λ^​(t)\widehat{\lambda}(t). Let x^\widehat{x} denote an optimal primal solution to (9) under arrival rates λ^​(t)\widehat{\lambda}(t). We construct ξ\xi as follows:

ξm={x^m,if ​m∈ℳ+​(t),0,otherwise.\displaystyle\xi_{m}=\begin{cases}\widehat{x}_{m},&\text{if }m\in\mathcal{M}^{+}(t),\\[4.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

We first verify that ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t). For i∈[n]∖𝒬+​(t)i\in[n]\setminus\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t),

[M​ξ]i≤[M​x^]i≤λ^i​(t)=λib,\displaystyle[M\xi]_{i}\leq[M\widehat{x}]_{i}\leq\widehat{\lambda}_{i}(t)=\lambda^{b}_{i},

confirming ξ∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi\in\mathcal{X}(t).

Next, we compute [M​ξ]i[M\xi]_{i} for i∈ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t):

[M​ξ]i=∑j∈δ⁡(i)ξ(i,j)=∑j∈δ⁡(i)x^(i,j)=λ^i​(t)=λib+ϵn.\displaystyle[M\xi]_{i}=\sum_{j\in\delta(i)}\xi_{(i,j)}=\sum_{j\in\delta(i)}\widehat{x}_{(i,j)}=\widehat{\lambda}_{i}(t)=\lambda_{i}^{b}+\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}. (44)

Since U∗U^{*} remains optimal when λb\lambda^{b} is replaced by λ^​(t)\widehat{\lambda}(t), and the dual constraints of (10) do not involve the arrival rates, the set ℳg\mathcal{M}^{g} is the same for both problems. The second equality then holds for i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) as follows. If (i,j)∈ℳg(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{g}, then since i∈𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t) we have (i,j)∈ℳ+​(t)(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{+}(t), so ξ(i,j)=x^(i,j)\xi_{(i,j)}=\widehat{x}_{(i,j)}. If (i,j)∉ℳg(i,j)\notin\mathcal{M}^{g}, then complementary slackness gives x^(i,j)=0=ξ(i,j)\widehat{x}_{(i,j)}=0=\xi_{(i,j)}. The third equality holds because i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+} implies Ui∗>0U^{*}_{i}>0, which by complementary slackness forces [M​x^]i=λ^i​(t)[M\widehat{x}]_{i}=\widehat{\lambda}_{i}(t). The last equality holds by the definition of λ^​(t)\widehat{\lambda}(t), since i∈ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t)i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t). Finally, we establish the drift bound:

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​ξ⟩ℐ+\displaystyle\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} =−ϵn∑i∈ℐ+∩𝒬+​(t)qi(t)\displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\cap\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t)}q_{i}(t)
=−ϵn​‖q⁡(t)‖1,ℐ+\displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{1,\mathcal{I}^{+}}
≤−ϵn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+.\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}.

The first equality holds since the restricted inner product ignores the coordinates outside ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} and qi​(t)=0q_{i}(t)=0 for i∉𝒬+​(t)i\notin\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), together with (44). The second equality is the definition of ∥⋅∥1,ℐ+\|\cdot\|_{1,\mathcal{I}^{+}}, again because qi​(t)=0q_{i}(t)=0 off 𝒬+​(t)\mathcal{Q}^{+}(t), and the final inequality holds since ‖z‖1,ℐ+≥‖z‖ℐ+\|z\|_{1,\mathcal{I}^{+}}\geq\|z\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. ∎

B.3 Proofs for Section 5.3

We provide the proofs of the auxiliary lemmas used to establish Proposition 4.

B.3.1 Proof of Lemma 6

We begin with the bounded-jump property.

Proof of Lemma 6.

Since ∥⋅∥ℐ+\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} satisfies the triangle inequality, the reverse triangle inequality gives |‖q⁡(t+)‖ℐ+−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+|≤‖q⁡(t+)−q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\left|\|q(t+)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right|\leq\|q(t+)-q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. It therefore suffices to bound ‖q⁡(t+)−q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t+)-q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} by 11 at each of the two event types identified in Lemma 9, an arrival and an abandonment. Throughout we use ∥ek∥ℐ+=𝟏{k∈ℐ+}≤1\|e_{k}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\mathbf{1}\{k\in\mathcal{I}^{+}\}\leq 1.

Abandonment: If an agent of type ii abandons, the queue updates as q⁡(t+)=q⁡(t)−eiq(t+)=q(t)-e_{i}. Consequently, ‖q⁡(t+)−q⁡(t)‖ℐ+=‖ei‖ℐ+≤1\|q(t+)-q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\|e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 1.

Arrival: Consider the arrival of a type-ii agent. Algorithm 1 either attempts a match or leaves the agent in the queue.

  1. 1.

    No Match: If no match is executed, q⁡(t+)=q⁡(t)+eiq(t+)=q(t)+e_{i}. Hence, ‖q⁡(t+)−q⁡(t)‖ℐ+=‖ei‖ℐ+≤1\|q(t+)-q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\|e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 1.

  2. 2.

    Match Executed: The selected match involves the arriving type ii and a waiting type j≠ij\neq i, so M​xi​(t)=ei+ejMx^{i}(t)=e_{i}+e_{j} and q⁡(t+)=q⁡(t)+ei−(ei+ej)=q⁡(t)−ejq(t+)=q(t)+e_{i}-(e_{i}+e_{j})=q(t)-e_{j}. Hence ‖q⁡(t+)−q⁡(t)‖ℐ+=‖ej‖ℐ+≤1\|q(t+)-q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\|e_{j}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq 1.

In all cases, the jump size is bounded by 1. ∎

B.3.2 Proof of Lemma 7

Next, we use the negative drift bound for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2} in Proposition 3 to derive the drift bounds for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}.

Proof of Lemma 7.

Applying the generator (36) with f⁡(q)=‖q‖ℐ+f(q)=\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} yields

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} =∑i=1nλis​[‖q⁡(t)+ei−M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]+∑i∈ℐ+θi​qi​(t)​[‖q⁡(t)−ei‖ℐ+−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+],\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\bigl[\|q(t)+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr]+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\theta_{i}q_{i}(t)\bigl[\|q(t)-e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr], (45)

where the abandonment sum is restricted to i∈ℐ+i\in\mathcal{I}^{+} since abandonments from i∉ℐ+i\notin\mathcal{I}^{+} do not affect ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}. By Lemma 6, each jump satisfies |‖q⁡(t+)‖ℐ+−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+|≤1|\|q(t^{+})\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}|\leq 1, so

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≤s+‖θ‖ℐ+​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq s+\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}, (46)

where we use ∑i=1nλis=s​‖λb‖1=s\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}=s\|\lambda^{b}\|_{1}=s and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

To obtain negative drift for large queue lengths, we use the inequality ‖a‖−‖b‖≤‖a‖2−‖b‖22​‖b‖\|a\|-\|b\|\leq\frac{\|a\|^{2}-\|b\|^{2}}{2\|b\|}, valid for any b≠0b\neq 0. Applying this to each term in (45), we have

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}} ≤∑i=1nλis​‖q⁡(t)+ei−M​xi​(t)‖ℐ+2−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+22​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ++∑i∈ℐ+θi​qi​(t)​‖q⁡(t)−ei‖ℐ+2−‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+22​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{s}\frac{\|q(t)+e_{i}-Mx^{i}(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}}{2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{+}}\theta_{i}q_{i}(t)\frac{\|q(t)-e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}-\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}}{2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}
=ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+22​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+,\displaystyle=\frac{\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}}{2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}},

where the equality holds since the numerator is the generator (36) with f⁡(q)=‖q‖ℐ+2f(q)=\|q\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. By Proposition 3, ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2≤2​s​(−εn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ++12)\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}\leq 2s(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}+\frac{1}{2}). Substituting yields

ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≤s⁡(−εn+12​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq s\left(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{n}}+\frac{1}{2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}\right). (47)

When ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≥nε\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}, the second term in (47) is at most ε2​n\frac{\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}}, yielding ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≤−s​ε2​n\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq-\frac{s\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n}}. When ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+<nε\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}<\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\varepsilon}, substituting into (46) gives ℒ​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+≤s+n​‖θ‖ℐ+ε\mathcal{L}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq s+\frac{\sqrt{n}\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}{\varepsilon}.

Finally, we prove Lemma 8, which establishes a uniform bound on the expected value of a function under the stated drift and jump conditions.

B.4 Bounded Dual Solutions

We state and prove Lemma 11, which bounds an optimal dual solution of the fluid LP.

Lemma 11.

Let U∗U^{*} be any optimal solution of (10) at arrival rates λb\lambda^{b}. Then

‖U∗‖∞≤r~max,‖U∗‖≤n​r~max.\|U^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\widetilde{r}_{\max},\qquad\|U^{*}\|\leq\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}.

Fix k∈𝒩k\in\mathcal{N}, and suppose that Uk∗>r~maxU_{k}^{*}>\widetilde{r}_{\max}. Define

U′=U∗−(Uk∗−r~max)​ek.U^{\prime}=U^{*}-(U_{k}^{*}-\widetilde{r}_{\max})e_{k}.

For every match m=(k,j)m=(k,j), we have

Uk′+Uj′=r~max+Uj∗≥r~m.U^{\prime}_{k}+U^{\prime}_{j}=\widetilde{r}_{\max}+U_{j}^{*}\geq\widetilde{r}_{m}.

All other dual constraints are unchanged, and U′≥0U^{\prime}\geq 0, so U′U^{\prime} is dual feasible. However,

(λb)⊤​U′−(λb)⊤​U∗=−λkb​(Uk∗−r~max)<0,(\lambda^{b})^{\top}U^{\prime}-(\lambda^{b})^{\top}U^{*}=-\lambda_{k}^{b}(U_{k}^{*}-\widetilde{r}_{\max})<0,

contradicting the optimality of U∗U^{*}. Since kk is arbitrary,

‖U∗‖∞≤r~max,‖U∗‖2≤n​‖U∗‖∞2≤n​r~max2.\|U^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\widetilde{r}_{\max},\qquad\|U^{*}\|^{2}\leq n\|U^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq n\widetilde{r}_{\max}^{2}.

In this section, we prove the regret bound in Proposition 1 without the GPG condition. We first establish an O⁡(s)O(\sqrt{s}) bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}], and then use this bound to derive the regret guarantee.

Under the GPG condition, the proof of Proposition 3 shows that

⟨q⁡(t),λb−M​x¯b​(t)⟩ℐ+≤−εn​‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+,\langle q(t),\lambda^{b}-M\overline{x}^{b}(t)\rangle_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\leq-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{n}}\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}},

which provides a downward drift contribution for ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. Without the GPG condition, we obtain the weaker bound

Thus, this term remains nonpositive and does not contribute to the growth of ‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. Following a proof strategy similar to that of Lemma 5, we construct an auxiliary vector ξ⁡(t)∈𝒳⁡(t)\xi(t)\in\mathcal{X}(t) to establish this bound in Lemma 12.

(M​ξ​(t))i≤(M​x∗)i≤λib.(M\xi(t))_{i}\leq(Mx^{*})_{i}\leq\lambda_{i}^{b}.

Next, we combine Lemma 12 with the downward drift induced by abandonment to establish an O⁡(s)O(\sqrt{s}) bound on 𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]\mathbb{E}[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}] in Lemma 13.

Lemma 13.

Let θmin=mini∈𝒩⁡θi>0\theta_{\min}=\min_{i\in\mathcal{N}}\theta_{i}>0. For every t≥0t\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2]≤sθmin​(1−e−θmin​t).\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}\bigr]\leq\frac{s}{\theta_{\min}}\bigl(1-e^{-\theta_{\min}t}\bigr).

supt≥0𝔼⁡[‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+]≤sθmin.\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\bigr]\leq\sqrt{\frac{s}{\theta_{\min}}}.

Define V⁡(q⁡(t))=‖q⁡(t)‖ℐ+2V(q(t))=\|q(t)\|_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}^{2}. Combining the expansion (38) in the proof of Lemma 3 with the bound (40), and using λs=s​λb\lambda^{s}=s\lambda^{b} and x¯​(t)=s​x¯b​(t)\overline{x}(t)=s\overline{x}^{b}(t), gives

The first term is nonpositive by Lemma 12. Since qi​(t)q_{i}(t) is a nonnegative integer, qi​(t)​[−2​qi​(t)+1]≤−qi​(t)2q_{i}(t)\bigl[-2q_{i}(t)+1\bigr]\leq-q_{i}(t)^{2}. Hence

dd​t​𝔼​[V⁡(q⁡(t))]≤s−θmin​𝔼​[V⁡(q⁡(t))].\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\mathbb{E}[V(q(t))]\leq s-\theta_{\min}\mathbb{E}[V(q(t))].

Having already expressed the regret in terms of the queue lengths in Proposition 2, we now combine this representation with the queue-length bound in Lemma 13 to prove Proposition 1.

Proof of Proposition 1.

ρT,sπ=1−ℛT,sπs​F∗​(λb)≥1−(T−1+‖θ‖∞)​n​r~maxF∗​(λb)​θmin​1s.\rho_{T,s}^{\pi}=1-\frac{\mathcal{R}_{T,s}^{\pi}}{sF^{*}(\lambda^{b})}\geq 1-\frac{(T^{-1}+\|\theta\|_{\infty})\sqrt{n}\,\widetilde{r}_{\max}}{F^{*}(\lambda^{b})\sqrt{\theta_{\min}}}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}.
